notes.h: Formation: agreement, consideration, intention and certainty
notes.body:
A contract needs agreement (offer and acceptance), consideration, an intention to create legal relations and sufficiently certain terms. Agreement is judged objectively.

Offer and acceptance
- An offer is a definite willingness to be bound once accepted; an invitation to treat only invites offers. Shelf displays (Pharmaceutical Society v Boots (1953)) and most adverts (Partridge v Crittenden (1968)) are invitations to treat, but a reward-style advert can be a unilateral offer to the world (Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893)).
- A counter-offer destroys the original offer (Hyde v Wrench (1840)); a request for information does not (Stevenson v McLean (1880)). In a battle of the forms the last shot usually wins (Butler v Ex-Cell-O (1979); Tekdata v Amphenol (2009)).
- Acceptance must be communicated. Silence is not acceptance (Felthouse v Bindley (1862)). Instantaneous acceptance takes effect on receipt (Entores (1955); Brinkibon (1983)); posted acceptance on posting (Adams v Lindsell (1818)), unless excluded or absurd (Holwell v Hughes (1974)).
- Revocation is effective only when communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880)), possibly through a reliable third party (Dickinson v Dodds (1876)). A unilateral offer should not be revoked once performance has begun (Errington (1952)).

Consideration
It must be sufficient but need not be adequate (Chappell v Nestlé (1960)), and it must not be past (Re McArdle (1951)), subject to Pao On (1980). Performing an existing duty is not consideration (Stilk v Myrick (1809)) unless the promisor gains a practical benefit without duress (Williams v Roffey (1991)). Part payment of a debt is not good consideration (Foakes v Beer (1884); Re Selectmove (1995)), but promissory estoppel may suspend the creditor's rights (High Trees (1947)). Estoppel is a shield, not a sword (Combe v Combe (1951)). MWB v Rock (2018) upheld 'no oral modification' clauses and left the Foakes/Roffey tension open.

Intention and certainty
Domestic agreements are presumed not binding (Balfour v Balfour (1919)) and commercial ones binding (Edwards v Skyways (1964)). Vague terms defeat a contract (Scammell v Ouston (1941)), but courts strive to uphold commercial deals (Hillas v Arcos (1932); Wells v Devani (2019)). A bare agreement to negotiate is unenforceable (Walford v Miles (1992)).

Worked example: A posts an offer on 1 May and a revocation on 3 May; B posts acceptance on 4 May and receives the revocation on 5 May. There is a contract, because acceptance was complete on posting and the revocation was not yet communicated.

Exam pitfalls
- Applying the postal rule to revocations: it never applies.
- Treating a promise to keep an offer open as binding without payment for it.
- Extending Roffey's practical benefit to part payment of debts.

Terms and incorporation
Whether a statement is a term or a mere representation depends on objective intention, weighing special knowledge (Oscar Chess v Williams (1957) against Dick Bentley v Harold Smith (1965)), importance and timing.
- Signature binds, read or not (L'Estrange v Graucob (1934)), unless the effect was misrepresented (Curtis v Chemical Cleaning (1951)).
- Unsigned terms need reasonable notice before or at contracting (Parker v SE Railway (1877); Olley v Marlborough Court (1949)), in a document a reasonable person expects to contain terms (Chapelton v Barry UDC (1940)).
- Onerous or unusual terms need special notice (Interfoto v Stiletto (1989); Thornton v Shoe Lane (1971); Lord Denning's 'red hand' in Spurling v Bradshaw (1956)).
- Course of dealing must be regular and consistent (Hollier v Rambler (1972); McCutcheon v MacBrayne (1964)).

Interpretation
The court asks what the words would mean to a reasonable person with the background knowledge reasonably available to both parties (ICS v West Bromwich (1998)). Arnold v Britton (2015) stresses that the natural meaning of clear words prevails, and commercial common sense cannot rescue a party from a bad bargain. Where words are genuinely ambiguous, the more commercially sensible reading is preferred (Rainy Sky (2011)). Wood v Capita (2017) treats text and context as tools in one iterative process. Pre-contract negotiations are excluded (Prenn v Simmonds (1971); Chartbrook (2009)), as is later conduct (James Miller v Whitworth (1970)). Obvious drafting errors can be corrected by construction (Chartbrook).

Implied terms
- In fact: only if necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying, never merely because it is reasonable, and never contradicting an express term (Marks & Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015)).
- In law: default incidents of a type of contract (Liverpool CC v Irwin (1977); Scally v Southern Health Board (1992)).
- By statute: SGA 1979 ss12–15 for non-consumer sales; Consumer Rights Act 2015 ss9–17 and s49 for consumers.
- Good faith is not a general duty, but may be implied in relational contracts (Yam Seng (2013)), and contractual discretions must be exercised rationally (Braganza v BP Shipping (2015)).

Worked example: a lease clause raising a service charge by 8% a year compound is enforced as written (Arnold). A negotiating email calling it a 'placeholder' is inadmissible on meaning, though it might support rectification or estoppel.

Exam pitfalls
- Saying ICS lets context override clear words; Arnold limits that.
- Using fairness as the test for implication in fact.
- Forgetting that an entire agreement clause excludes collateral warranties but not, by itself, misrepresentation liability.

notes.h: Exemption clauses: construction, UCTA 1977 and the CRA 2015
notes.body:
An exemption clause must clear three hurdles: incorporation, construction and statutory control.

Construction
- Ambiguity is read against the party relying on the clause (contra proferentem), now applied sparingly between commercial equals. Limitation clauses are read less strictly than total exclusions (Ailsa Craig v Malvern (1983)).
- Negligence: an express reference works. Otherwise general words cover negligence only if wide enough and there is no realistic other head of liability (Canada Steamship (1952)), treated today as guidance (HIH v Chase Manhattan (2003)). Clear words are needed to remove valuable rights (Triple Point v PTT (2021)).
- There is no rule that a fundamental breach defeats an exclusion; it is a matter of construction (Photo Production v Securicor (1980)).

UCTA 1977 (mainly business-to-business since 2015)
- s2(1): no exclusion of liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence. s2(2): other negligence losses only if reasonable.
- s3: on written standard terms, exclusion for breach, or a right to perform substantially differently, must be reasonable.
- s6: title (SGA s12) can never be excluded; ss13–15 only if reasonable (s6(1A)).
- Reasonableness is judged at contracting, with the burden on the party relying on the clause (s11(1), (5)). Sch 2 factors include bargaining power, inducement and knowledge; s11(4) adds resources and insurance for caps. Compare George Mitchell v Finney Lock (1983), where the cap was unreasonable, with Watford Electronics v Sanderson (2001), where courts deferred to negotiated terms between equals.

Consumer Rights Act 2015, Part 2
- s62: a term is unfair if, contrary to good faith, it causes a significant imbalance to the consumer's detriment. Good faith means fair and open dealing (DGFT v First National Bank (2001)). Unfair terms do not bind the consumer (s62(1)), the rest of the contract continues so far as practicable (s67), and the court must consider fairness itself (s71).
- s64: terms on main subject matter and price are exempt only if transparent and prominent, and not if they are on the Sch 2 grey list.
- Blacklisted: excluding the statutory goods rights (s31) and core service rights (s57), and excluding liability for negligently caused death or personal injury (s65).

Worked example: a large supplier's standard terms cap liability at the price paid and exclude crop loss. The farmer customer suffers £240,000 of loss from a bug the supplier knew about. The clause is incorporated by signature and probably covers the loss, but under s3 and s11 the supplier's insurance, the unequal bargaining power and its knowledge of the defect point towards unreasonableness (George Mitchell).

Exam pitfalls
- Applying UCTA to a consumer contract: use the CRA.
- Skipping incorporation and construction.
- Forgetting who bears the burden of proving reasonableness.

notes.h: Vitiating factors: misrepresentation, mistake, duress, undue influence, illegality
notes.body:
Misrepresentation
An unambiguous false statement of existing fact or law that induces the contract. Opinion is not usually enough (Bisset v Wilkinson (1927)), unless the speaker has superior knowledge (Smith v Land & House (1884)). A false statement of intention is a statement of fact (Edgington v Fitzmaurice (1885)). Silence is not generally a misrepresentation (Keates v Cadogan (1851)), but half-truths (Dimmock v Hallett (1866)) and statements that become false before the contract (With v O'Flanagan (1936)) are. Failing to check is no defence (Redgrave v Hurd (1881)), nor is suspicion (Hayward v Zurich (2016)).
- Fraud (Derry v Peek (1889)): deceit damages cover all direct loss (Doyle v Olby (1969); Smith New Court (1997)).
- MA 1967 s2(1): the defendant must prove reasonable belief (Howard Marine v Ogden (1978)). Damages are measured as for fraud (Royscot v Rogerson (1991)), a criticised result.
- Rescission is barred by affirmation, lapse of time, third-party rights or impossibility of restitution. s2(2) allows damages instead of rescission. s3 subjects exclusion clauses to UCTA reasonableness (First Tower Trustees (2018)).

Mistake
Common mistake voids a contract only if it makes performance essentially different (Bell v Lever Bros (1932); Great Peace (2002), which rejected Solle v Butcher's equitable rescission). Compare Couturier v Hastie (1856) with McRae (1951). Unilateral mistake as to terms known to the other party prevents a contract (Hartog v Colin & Shields (1939)); a mistake about quality alone does not (Smith v Hughes (1871)). On identity, a written contract with a named person is void (Shogun Finance v Hudson (2003)), while face-to-face dealing is merely voidable (Phillips v Brooks (1919); Lewis v Averay (1972)). Rectification needs an actual, outwardly expressed common intention (FSHC v GLAS (2019)).

Duress and undue influence
Economic duress requires illegitimate pressure that significantly caused the contract, judged by whether there was a practical alternative (Universe Tankships (1983); Atlas Express v Kafco (1989)). Lawful act duress is very narrow (PIAC v Times Travel (2021)). Undue influence is actual or presumed (RBS v Etridge (No 2) (2001)). A lender is put on inquiry by non-commercial surety arrangements and must take reasonable steps; joint loans do not trigger this (CIBC v Pitt (1994)).

Illegality follows a policy-based, proportionality approach (Patel v Mirza (2016)).

Worked example: a dealer states a van's mileage as 40,000 without checking a file showing 110,000. Probably not fraud, but s2(1) liability is likely (no reasonable grounds). Continued use risks affirmation.

Exam pitfalls
- Calling misrepresentation 'void'; it makes the contract voidable.
- Citing Solle v Butcher as good law.
- Forgetting that s2(1) reverses the burden of proof.

Frustration discharges a contract automatically when, without either party's fault, a supervening event makes performance radically different from what was undertaken (Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC (1956)).

Categories and illustrations
- Destruction of subject matter: Taylor v Caldwell (1863), music hall burned down (the older implied-condition theory).
- Frustration of common purpose: Krell v Henry (1903), coronation procession cancelled, frustrated; Herne Bay v Hutton (1903), fleet still there to be seen, not frustrated.
- Increased cost or delay alone is not enough: Davis Contractors; Tsakiroglou v Noblee Thorl (1962), Suez closure.
- Leases can in principle be frustrated but rarely are (National Carriers v Panalpina (1981); Canary Wharf v EMA (2019), Brexit).
- The Sea Angel (2007): a multi-factorial approach weighing terms, context, risk allocation and whether enforcement would be unjust.

Limits
- Self-induced events do not frustrate (Maritime National Fish (1935); The Super Servant Two (1990), where choosing which contract to perform was an election).
- Foreseen and allocated risks, including events covered by a force majeure clause, exclude frustration (Amalgamated Investment v John Walker (1977)). A duty to use reasonable endeavours did not require accepting payment in a non-contractual currency (MUR Shipping v RTI (2024)).

Consequences
At common law the contract ends from the event. Accrued obligations remain and future ones are discharged (Chandler v Webster (1904)). Fibrosa (1943) allowed recovery only for total failure of consideration. The Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 now applies:
- s1(2): money paid is recoverable and money payable ceases to be payable. The court may allow the payee to keep or recover expenses, up to the sums paid or payable before discharge (Gamerco v ICM (1995), a broad discretion).
- s1(3): a just sum for a valuable non-money benefit, capped at the benefit's value (BP v Hunt (No 2) (1979), valued as the end product reduced by the frustrating event).
- s2(5) excludes voyage charters and carriage of goods by sea, insurance, and perishing of specific goods. Parties may contract out (s2(3)).

Worked example: a venue hire costs £90,000, with £30,000 paid and £60,000 due later. The venue is destroyed by an accidental fire. The contract is frustrated (Taylor v Caldwell). The hirer recovers the £30,000 and the £60,000 ceases to be due. If just, the court may let the owner keep up to £8,000 of the £30,000 for expenses (capped at sums paid or payable before discharge). The hirer's £20,000 spending gives the owner no benefit, so s1(3) is unlikely to help.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating expense or delay as frustration.
- Thinking a party 'elects' to frustrate; discharge is automatic.
- Applying s1(2) expenses beyond the sums paid or payable before discharge.

notes.h: Breach, classification of terms and termination
notes.body:
A breach is a failure, without lawful excuse, to perform any contractual obligation, whether by non-performance, defective performance or repudiation. Liability is usually strict.

Classification of terms
- Condition: any breach allows termination plus damages (Poussard v Spiers (1876)).
- Warranty: damages only (Bettini v Gye (1876)).
- Innominate term: termination only if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit (Hongkong Fir (1962); The Hansa Nord (1976)).
- A term is a condition by statute (SGA 1979 ss12–15), by precedent or by clear designation, though a label is not conclusive if the result would be absurd (Schuler v Wickman (1974)). Time clauses in mercantile contracts are usually conditions (Bunge v Tradax (1981)). In non-consumer sales, s15A stops rejection for slight breaches of ss13–15, reversing the strictness of Arcos v Ronaasen (1933).
- Time of the essence: Union Eagle v Golden Achievement (1997). A clause making punctual payment of the essence makes any late payment repudiatory (Lombard v Butterworth (1987)).

Anticipatory breach and election
A clear renunciation before performance is due is an immediate breach (Hochster v De la Tour (1853)), tested by how a reasonable person would see it (Eminence v Heaney (2010)). The innocent party then elects.
- Terminate: acceptance must be clear but can be by conduct, including non-performance (Vitol v Norelf (1996)). Future primary obligations end, damages replace them, and accrued rights and surviving clauses remain (Photo Production (1980)).
- Affirm: the contract continues for both sides, so the repudiator can rely on later events (The Simona (1989)). A party may perform and claim the price if it needs no cooperation and has a legitimate interest (White & Carter v McGregor (1962)). There is no such interest where damages are adequate and performing would be wholly unreasonable (The Alaskan Trader (1984)).

Entire obligations
Partial performance earns nothing (Cutter v Powell (1795); Sumpter v Hedges (1898)) unless there is substantial performance, in which case the price is payable less the cost of remedying defects (Hoenig v Isaacs (1952); compare Bolton v Mahadeva (1972)).

Worked example: a supply contract says 'delivery by the 5th is a condition'. One delivery arrives on the 6th. The buyer may terminate, even though the real motive is a falling market, because breach of a condition allows termination whatever the consequences. Dented but usable tins under a 'good condition' term are probably a breach of an innominate term, giving damages only.

Exam pitfalls
- Assuming any serious-sounding breach justifies termination; classify the term first.
- Forgetting that an innocent party who wrongly terminates may itself repudiate.
- Treating White & Carter as unlimited.

notes.h: Remedies: damages, limits, agreed sums and equitable relief
notes.body:
Damages aim to put the claimant, so far as money can, where performance would have left it (Robinson v Harman (1848)).

Measures
- Expectation: loss of bargain, or the reasonable cost of cure; where cure is disproportionate, a modest loss-of-amenity award instead (Ruxley v Forsyth (1996)).
- Reliance: wasted expenditure, including foreseeable pre-contract spending (Anglia TV v Reed (1972)), but not to escape a bad bargain (C & P Haulage (1983); Omak Maritime (2010)).
- Loss of a chance: Chaplin v Hicks (1911).
- Non-pecuniary loss: generally none (Addis v Gramophone (1909)), except where a major object of the contract is pleasure or peace of mind (Jarvis v Swans Tours (1973); Farley v Skinner (2001)).

Limits
- Remoteness: loss arising naturally (limb 1) or contemplated by both parties because of special knowledge (limb 2) (Hadley v Baxendale (1854); Victoria Laundry (1949)). The contract test is 'not unlikely', stricter than the tort test (The Heron II (1969)). The type, not the extent, of loss must be contemplated (Parsons v Uttley Ingham (1978)). Assumption of responsibility may matter in unusual cases (The Achilleas (2008); Sylvia Shipping (2010)).
- Mitigation: no recovery for avoidable loss (British Westinghouse (1912); Payzu v Saunders (1919)).
- Contributory negligence applies only where the contractual duty mirrors a tort duty of care (Vesta v Butcher (1988)).
- Assessment is normally at breach, subject to later events (The Golden Victory (2007); Bunge v Nidera (2015)).

Agreed sums and penalties
A claim for the price is a debt: no loss need be proved and mitigation is irrelevant. A clause triggered by breach is a penalty if it is out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance (Cavendish v Makdessi; ParkingEye v Beavis (2015)).

Gain-based and equitable remedies
- Negotiating damages only where a valuable asset-like right is lost and ordinary loss is not quantifiable (Morris-Garner v One Step (2018); Wrotham Park (1974)).
- An account of profits is exceptional (AG v Blake (2001)).
- Specific performance is discretionary and given where damages are inadequate (land, unique goods; Beswick v Beswick (1968)), but not for personal service or constant supervision (Co-op v Argyll (1998)). Negative injunctions are granted unless they would compel performance (Lumley v Wagner (1852); Warner Bros v Nelson (1937); Page One v Britton (1968)).

Worked example: a camera arrives a week late. The disclosed £12,000 wedding fee is limb 2 loss, but a £500 hire would have avoided it, so mitigation limits recovery to about £500. The undisclosed magazine deal is too remote.

Exam pitfalls
- Using 'genuine pre-estimate' as the sole penalty test.
- Confusing the contract and tort remoteness tests.

cards.b: An offer is a definite expression of willingness to be bound on stated terms as soon as the other party accepts; an invitation to treat merely invites offers or negotiation. The distinction is judged objectively, from how a reasonable person would read the communication.

cards.f: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (1953)
cards.b: Goods on self-service shelves are an invitation to treat. The customer makes the offer at the till and the cashier accepts, so the sale took place under a pharmacist's supervision.

A newspaper advertisement of birds for sale was an invitation to treat, so the advertiser had not 'offered for sale' a protected bird. Bilateral advertisements are usually invitations to treat because the seller's stock is limited.

cards.f: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co (1893)
cards.b: An advertisement promising £100 to anyone who caught flu after using the smoke ball as directed, backed by a £1,000 bank deposit, was a unilateral offer to the world. It was accepted by performing the conditions, and notice of acceptance was impliedly waived.

A counter-offer rejects and destroys the original offer: Hyde v Wrench (1840), where an offer to buy at £950 killed an offer to sell at £1,000. A mere request for information, such as asking whether delivery could be spread over a longer period, leaves the offer open: Stevenson, Jaques & Co v McLean (1880).

Each side sends its own standard terms. Butler Machine Tool v Ex-Cell-O (1979) applied traditional offer and counter-offer analysis, so the 'last shot' usually wins. Tekdata Interconnections v Amphenol (2009) confirms that this is the default unless the parties' conduct clearly shows a different common intention.

Acceptance by post is complete when the letter is properly posted, provided post is a reasonable or contemplated way to accept: Adams v Lindsell (1818). It applies even if the letter is delayed or lost: Household Fire Insurance v Grant (1879).

cards.f: When is the postal rule displaced?
cards.b: The offeror can exclude it, for example by requiring actual 'notice in writing'. It also does not apply where it would cause manifest inconvenience or absurdity: Holwell Securities v Hughes (1974). It never applies to revocations of offers.

Acceptance by telex or phone takes effect when and where it is received: Entores v Miles Far East (1955); Brinkibon v Stahag Stahl (1983). Lord Wilberforce said there is no universal rule. The answer depends on the parties' intentions, sound business practice and where the risk should lie.

An uncle wrote that if he heard nothing more he would consider his nephew's horse his. Silence was not acceptance, because an offeror cannot impose a contract on someone just because they fail to reply.

An offer can be revoked at any time before acceptance, even if it was promised to stay open (unless that promise was paid for). Revocation takes effect only when it is communicated: Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880). Communication through a reliable third party is enough: Dickinson v Dodds (1876).

cards.f: Revoking a unilateral offer once performance has begun
cards.b: Once the offeree has begun to perform, the offeror is under an implied obligation not to revoke: Errington v Errington (1952); Daulia v Four Millbank Nominees (1978), obiter. Offers made to the world can be revoked by taking reasonable steps to publicise the revocation: Shuey v United States (1875).

Some right, interest, profit or benefit to one party, or some forbearance, detriment, loss or responsibility given or suffered by the other: Currie v Misa (1875). In Dunlop v Selfridge (1915) it was described as the price for which the other's promise is bought.

cards.f: Consideration must be sufficient but need not be adequate
cards.b: The court does not weigh the value of what is exchanged. In Chappell & Co v Nestlé (1960), used chocolate wrappers formed part of the consideration. In Thomas v Thomas (1842), a rent of £1 a year was good consideration.

An act done before the promise is not consideration for it: Re McArdle (1951). The exception, from Lampleigh v Brathwait (1615) as restated in Pao On v Lau Yiu Long (1980), needs three things: the act was done at the promisor's request, both understood it would be paid for, and the payment would have been legally enforceable.

A main contractor promised a subcontractor extra money to finish carpentry work on time, and the promise was enforceable. The promisor obtained a 'practical benefit', such as avoiding a delay penalty, and there was no duress or fraud. This qualified the strict rule in Stilk v Myrick (1809).

cards.f: Foakes v Beer (1884) and part payment of debts
cards.b: A creditor's promise to accept part payment in full settlement does not bind, because paying less than is due gives no consideration. Pinnel's Case exceptions: payment early, at a different place, or with something extra, all at the creditor's request. Re Selectmove (1995) refused to extend Roffey's practical benefit to part payment.

cards.f: MWB Business Exchange Centres v Rock Advertising (2018)
cards.b: The Supreme Court held that 'no oral modification' clauses are legally effective, so an oral variation that does not comply has no effect. It declined to decide whether Foakes v Beer survives Williams v Roffey, while saying the issue may need reconsidering.

Requirements: a pre-existing legal relationship, a clear and unequivocal promise not to enforce strict legal rights, reliance by the promisee, and that it would be inequitable for the promisor to go back on the promise. Authorities: Hughes v Metropolitan Railway (1877); Central London Property Trust v High Trees House (1947).

It is a shield, not a sword, so it cannot create a new cause of action: Combe v Combe (1951). It does not apply where the promise was extracted by pressure: D & C Builders v Rees (1966). It is generally suspensory, so strict rights can be resumed for the future on reasonable notice: Tool Metal Manufacturing v Tungsten Electric (1955).

cards.f: Intention to create legal relations: presumptions
cards.b: Domestic and social agreements are presumed not to be binding: Balfour v Balfour (1919). The presumption is rebutted, for example, for separating spouses: Merritt v Merritt (1970). Commercial agreements are presumed binding, and the burden of rebutting this is heavy: Edwards v Skyways (1964).

An express statement that an agreement is binding in honour only displaces legal intent: Rose & Frank Co v JR Crompton & Bros (1925). A comfort letter saying it is a parent's 'policy' to ensure its subsidiary pays was a statement of present policy, not a contractual promise: Kleinwort Benson v Malaysia Mining Corp (1989).

Terms that are too vague prevent a contract: Scammell v Ouston (1941), 'on hire-purchase terms'. Courts try to give effect to commercial agreements, using past dealings or a mechanism in the contract: Hillas v Arcos (1932). A bare agreement to negotiate, even in good faith, is unenforceable: Walford v Miles (1992).

cards.f: RTS Flexible Systems v Molkerei Alois Müller (2010) and Wells v Devani (2019)
cards.b: RTS: a contract can be inferred from conduct despite a 'subject to contract' label, where all essential terms were agreed and the parties waived the label. Wells: an estate agent's oral agreement was complete even though it did not say when commission became payable, because, read objectively, commission was payable on completion of a purchase by the introduced buyer; if necessary, such a term would also have been implied.

The test is whether, objectively, the statement was intended to be a binding promise. Relevant factors: special knowledge (Oscar Chess v Williams (1957), private seller, a representation; Dick Bentley v Harold Smith (1965), dealer, a term), the importance of the statement, and the time gap before the contract (Routledge v McKay (1954)).

A person who signs a contractual document is bound by its terms whether or not they read them. The exception is fraud or misrepresentation, for example where the effect of a clause was misstated: Curtis v Chemical Cleaning & Dyeing Co (1951).

Unsigned terms are incorporated if reasonable notice was given before or at the time the contract was made: Parker v South Eastern Railway (1877). A notice in a hotel bedroom came too late: Olley v Marlborough Court (1949). A document that a reasonable person would see as a mere receipt does not carry terms: Chapelton v Barry UDC (1940).

cards.f: Interfoto Picture Library v Stiletto Visual Programmes (1989)
cards.b: A particularly onerous or unusual term must be fairly and reasonably brought to the other party's attention. Here, a steep holding fee for late-returned photographic transparencies was not incorporated. This develops Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking (1971) and Lord Denning's 'red hand' remark in Spurling v Bradshaw (1956).

Terms can be incorporated through a regular and consistent course of past dealings. Three or four dealings over five years were not enough for a consumer: Hollier v Rambler Motors (1972). Inconsistent past practice is also insufficient: McCutcheon v David MacBrayne (1964).

cards.f: Investors Compensation Scheme v West Bromwich BS (1998)
cards.b: Lord Hoffmann: interpretation asks what meaning the document would convey to a reasonable person with all the background knowledge reasonably available to the parties when they contracted. This excludes prior negotiations and statements of subjective intent.

Service charges rose by 10% a year compound, producing absurd sums. Lord Neuberger held that the natural meaning of the words is central, and that commercial common sense must not be used to undervalue the language or to rescue a party from a bad bargain. The clause was enforced as written.

Lord Hodge: textualism and contextualism are tools, not rival camps. Interpretation is one iterative process, and how much weight each tool gets depends on the document's nature, complexity and drafting quality.

cards.f: Rainy Sky SA v Kookmin Bank (2011)
cards.b: Where a term can reasonably bear two meanings, the court should prefer the one more consistent with business common sense. Here that favoured reading bonds as covering refunds on the shipbuilder's insolvency.

Evidence of pre-contractual negotiations is inadmissible to show what the terms mean: Prenn v Simmonds (1971); Chartbrook v Persimmon Homes (2009). So is the parties' later conduct: James Miller & Partners v Whitworth Street Estates (1970). Negotiations can still prove that a background fact was known, or support a rectification or estoppel claim.

Where it is clear that something has gone wrong with the language, and clear what a reasonable person would have understood the parties to mean, the court can read the contract that way without rectification. In Chartbrook (2009), a price formula was read so it made commercial sense.

cards.f: Terms implied in fact: Marks & Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015)
cards.b: A term is implied only if it is necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying (the officious bystander test from Shirlaw v Southern Foundries (1939)). Being reasonable or fair is not enough. The test is applied at the time of contracting, and an implied term cannot contradict an express one.

These are default terms implied into all contracts of a defined type as a necessary incident of that relationship, on wider policy grounds. Liverpool City Council v Irwin (1977): a landlord must take reasonable care of the common parts of a tower block. Scally v Southern Health Board (1992): a duty to tell employees about valuable pension rights.

For non-consumer sales of goods, the Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss12–15 imply terms on title, description, satisfactory quality, fitness for purpose and sample. For consumer contracts, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 ss9–17 treat equivalent terms as included (e.g. quality s9, fitness s10, description s11, title s17), and s49 requires services to be performed with reasonable care and skill.

cards.f: Good faith in English contract law
cards.b: There is no general duty of good faith. A duty may be implied in 'relational' contracts: Yam Seng v International Trade Corp (2013). A contractual discretion must be exercised rationally and not arbitrarily or capriciously: Braganza v BP Shipping (2015).

cards.f: Parol evidence rule and entire agreement clauses
cards.b: Where a written document was intended to be the whole contract, extrinsic evidence cannot generally add to it, vary it or contradict it, though there are many exceptions. An entire agreement clause excludes collateral warranties, but on its own it does not exclude liability for misrepresentation.

cards.f: Three hurdles for an exemption clause
cards.b: (1) The clause must be incorporated. (2) On its true construction it must cover the loss in question. (3) It must survive statutory control under UCTA 1977 (non-consumer contracts) or the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (consumer contracts).

Ambiguity in an exemption clause is resolved against the party relying on it. Limitation clauses are read less strictly than total exclusions: Ailsa Craig Fishing v Malvern Fishing (1983). In commercial contracts between parties of equal strength, the rule is now used sparingly.

cards.f: Canada Steamship Lines v The King (1952)
cards.b: These are guidelines for excluding liability for negligence. An express reference to negligence works. Otherwise, general words cover negligence only if wide enough to do so and there is no realistic head of liability other than negligence that they could cover. Modern courts treat the guidelines as aids, not rigid rules: HIH Casualty v Chase Manhattan (2003).

A security patrolman lit a fire that destroyed the factory. The House of Lords rejected any rule of law that a fundamental breach defeats an exclusion clause. Whether a clause covers a breach, however serious, is a question of construction.

The Supreme Court held that liquidated damages for delay accrue up to termination. It also held that a clause will not readily be read as removing valuable rights such as damages for negligence without clear words. 'Negligence' in the cap's carve-out covered negligent breach of contract.

UCTA now controls exclusion of business liability (s1(3)) in non-consumer contracts, mainly business-to-business. Consumer contracts and consumer notices are governed by Part 2 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 instead.

s2(1): a contract term or notice cannot exclude or restrict liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence. s2(2): for other loss or damage caused by negligence, exclusion is allowed only if it satisfies the reasonableness requirement.

Where one party deals on the other's written standard terms of business, the other cannot exclude or restrict liability for breach, or claim to be entitled to perform substantially differently or not at all, except so far as the term is reasonable.

Liability for the implied term about title (Sale of Goods Act 1979 s12) can never be excluded. In non-consumer sales, the terms on description, quality, fitness and sample (ss13–15) can be excluded only so far as reasonable (s6(1A)).

The term must be fair and reasonable given the circumstances known or contemplated when the contract was made. The burden is on the party relying on it (s11(5)). Schedule 2 guidelines (formally for ss6–7, but applied generally): bargaining strength, any inducement, knowledge of the term, practicability of compliance, and for limitation caps, resources and insurance (s11(4)).

cards.f: George Mitchell (Chesterhall) v Finney Lock Seeds (1983)
cards.b: Limiting liability for defective cabbage seed to its price was unreasonable. Key factors: the sellers' practice of negotiating settlements, the negligence involved, and the fact that sellers could insure. Appellate courts should be slow to interfere with a trial judge's reasonableness assessment.

Where experienced businesses of roughly equal bargaining power negotiate terms, they are the best judges of commercial fairness. Courts should be reluctant to find a limitation clause unreasonable in that setting.

cards.f: Consumer Rights Act 2015 s62: the fairness test
cards.b: A term is unfair if, contrary to the requirement of good faith, it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' rights and obligations to the consumer's detriment. Fairness is judged by the subject matter, all the surrounding circumstances and the other terms. An unfair term does not bind the consumer, and the rest of the contract continues where practicable (s67).

Terms setting the main subject matter or the appropriateness of the price are not assessed for fairness, but only if they are transparent (plain, intelligible and legible) and prominent (brought to the average consumer's attention). The exemption does not cover terms on the Schedule 2 Part 1 grey list.

Traders cannot exclude the statutory rights for goods, such as satisfactory quality (s31), or the core statutory rights for services, such as reasonable care and skill (s57). Liability for death or personal injury from negligence cannot be excluded either (s65).

cards.f: Director General of Fair Trading v First National Bank (2001)
cards.b: Lord Bingham explained good faith as fair and open dealing: openness means terms that are clear, legible and free of traps, and fair dealing means not exploiting the consumer's weaker position. A term allowing contractual interest after judgment was held not unfair.

This is an indicative, non-exhaustive list of terms that may be unfair. Examples: letting the trader keep prepayments when the consumer cancels without matching compensation the other way, disproportionate compensation for consumer default, and unilateral changes by the trader without a valid reason.
An unambiguous false statement of existing fact or law, made by one party to the other, that induces the other to enter the contract. Misstatements of law are covered: Pankhania v Hackney LBC (2002).

An honest opinion is not usually a misrepresentation: Bisset v Wilkinson (1927), an estimate of sheep capacity on land never used for sheep. But an opinion from someone with superior knowledge may imply there are facts to support it: Smith v Land & House Property Corp (1884), a 'most desirable tenant' who was in arrears.

A false statement of present intention, about the purpose of a debenture issue, was a misrepresentation of fact. Bowen LJ said a person's state of mind is 'as much a fact as the state of his digestion'.

There is no general duty to disclose: Keates v Cadogan (1851). Exceptions: half-truths (Dimmock v Hallett (1866)); statements that become false before the contract and are not corrected (With v O'Flanagan (1936)); fiduciary relationships; and insurance, where business insureds now owe a statutory duty of fair presentation under the Insurance Act 2015.

It is no defence that the claimant could have discovered the truth: Redgrave v Hurd (1881). There is no inducement where the claimant relied on their own investigation: Attwood v Small (1838). The claimant need not have believed the statement was true, so suspicion does not defeat the claim: Hayward v Zurich Insurance (2016).

A false statement made knowingly, without belief in its truth, or recklessly not caring whether it is true: Derry v Peek (1889). Damages in the tort of deceit cover all loss flowing directly from the fraud, even unforeseeable loss: Doyle v Olby (1969); Smith New Court v Scrimgeour Vickers (1997).

The misrepresentor is liable in damages unless they prove they had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe up to the time of contract, that the statement was true. This reverses the burden of proof. In Howard Marine v Ogden (1978), relying on a Lloyd's Register error about barge capacity was not reasonable grounds.

Damages under s2(1) are measured as if the misrepresentation were fraudulent (the 'fiction of fraud'), so even unforeseeable losses are recoverable. This is widely criticised, and Lord Steyn reserved his view on it in Smith New Court (1997).

Misrepresentation makes the contract voidable, and rescission undoes it as if it had never been made. It is barred by affirmation (Long v Lloyd (1958)), lapse of time (Leaf v International Galleries (1950)), intervening third-party rights, or impossibility of restitution, though equity is flexible about restitution (Erlanger v New Sombrero Phosphate (1878)). For non-fraudulent misrepresentation, the court can award damages instead of rescission (s2(2) MA 1967).

Under s3 MA 1967, a term excluding or restricting liability for misrepresentation must satisfy the UCTA reasonableness test. A non-reliance clause can fall within s3: First Tower Trustees v CDS (Superstores International) (2018). A party can never exclude liability for its own fraud: S Pearson & Son v Dublin Corp (1907); HIH Casualty v Chase Manhattan (2003).

A shared mistake about quality makes the contract void only if it makes the subject matter essentially different from what was believed: Bell v Lever Bros (1932). Great Peace Shipping v Tsavliris Salvage (2002): the contract is void if performance is impossible in the way both parties contemplated, and there is no separate equitable power to rescind (Solle v Butcher disapproved).

cards.f: Res extincta: Couturier v Hastie (1856) and McRae v Commonwealth Disposals Commission (1951)
cards.b: Couturier: a sale of corn that had already been disposed of before the contract did not bind the buyer. McRae: the seller of a non-existent oil tanker had impliedly promised that it existed, so the seller was liable in damages.

Where one party knows the other is mistaken about a term, there is no contract: Hartog v Colin & Shields (1939), hare skins offered per pound instead of per piece. A mistake about quality (old or new oats) does not affect the contract unless the quality was a term: Smith v Hughes (1871).

Where a written contract names a specific person, a rogue posing as that person makes no contract, so it is void: Shogun Finance v Hudson (2003), decided 3–2. In face-to-face dealings, there is a strong presumption that the seller intends to deal with the person in front of them, so the contract is only voidable for fraud: Phillips v Brooks (1919); Lewis v Averay (1972).

cards.f: Rectification for common mistake: FSHC Group Holdings v GLAS Trust (2019)
cards.b: The Court of Appeal held that the claimant must show an actual common intention, outwardly expressed, that the written document fails to record. This is a subjective test, rejecting Lord Hoffmann's objective approach in Chartbrook, which was obiter.

There must be illegitimate pressure that was a significant cause of the contract, judged against whether the victim had a practical alternative: Universe Tankships v ITWF (1983); DSND Subsea v Petroleum Geo-Services (2000). In Atlas Express v Kafco (1989), a carrier's refusal to deliver unless paid more amounted to duress. The contract is voidable.

cards.f: Pakistan International Airline Corp v Times Travel (UK) Ltd (2021)
cards.b: Lawful act duress is very narrow. Lord Hodge (majority) confined it to morally reprehensible conduct, such as exploiting knowledge of criminal activity, or using illegitimate means to manoeuvre the claimant into a position of weakness to force it to waive a claim. Lord Burrows, concurring, preferred a 'bad faith demand' test. Hard bargaining with monopoly power, without more, is not enough.

Actual undue influence must be proved. In presumed cases, influence is inferred from a relationship of trust and confidence plus a transaction that calls for explanation. Some relationships automatically count as relationships of trust, such as solicitor and client or parent and child, but spouses do not.

A lender is put on inquiry whenever a person stands surety for another's debts in a non-commercial relationship. It is protected if it takes reasonable steps, usually getting a solicitor's confirmation that the surety was advised independently. A joint loan to a couple does not put the lender on inquiry: CIBC Mortgages v Pitt (1994).

On illegality, the Supreme Court replaced the old reliance test with a policy-based approach. The court asks: what is the purpose of the rule that was broken, what other relevant policies are engaged, and would denying the claim be proportionate?

Frustration happens when, without either party's fault, performance becomes radically different from what was undertaken. Labour shortages that made a housing contract slower and more expensive did not frustrate it, because extra cost or delay alone is not enough.
A music hall hired for concerts burned down before the performances. Both parties were excused, because the contract depended on the hall continuing to exist (an implied condition).

cards.f: Krell v Henry (1903) vs Herne Bay Steam Boat v Hutton (1903)
cards.b: Krell: hiring rooms to watch the coronation procession was frustrated when the procession was cancelled, because the viewing was the shared foundation of the contract. Herne Bay: hiring a boat to see the naval review and cruise round the fleet was not frustrated, because the fleet was still there to be seen.
Closure of the Suez Canal meant shipping goods around the Cape, a longer and more expensive route. Performance was not radically different, so the contract was not frustrated.

A party cannot rely on an event caused by its own choice. Maritime National Fish v Ocean Trawlers (1935): the defendant allocated its limited fishing licences to other boats. The Super Servant Two (1990): choosing which contract to perform after losing a vessel was the party's own election.

If the contract deals with the event, for example through a force majeure clause, or the risk was foreseen and allocated, the contract is not frustrated. In Amalgamated Investment & Property v John Walker (1977), the risk of a building being listed was part of the bargain the buyer took on.

Rix LJ described a 'multi-factorial' approach. The court looks at the terms, the contract's context, the parties' knowledge, expectations and assumptions, especially about risk at the time of contracting, and then asks whether holding the parties to the contract would be unjust.

A lease can in principle be frustrated, though this will rarely happen: National Carriers v Panalpina (1981). In Canary Wharf (BP4) T1 v European Medicines Agency (2019), Brexit and the agency's forced relocation did not frustrate its 25-year lease.

cards.f: Effects of frustration at common law
cards.b: The contract ends automatically from the frustrating event. Future obligations are discharged and accrued ones remain: Chandler v Webster (1904). Fibrosa v Fairbairn Lawson (1943) allowed recovery of an advance payment on total failure of consideration, but gave nothing for partial failure or for expenses.

Money paid before discharge can be recovered, and money payable before discharge stops being payable. If it is just, the court may let the payee keep or recover its expenses, capped at the amount paid or payable before discharge.

cards.f: LR(FC)A 1943 s1(3) and BP Exploration v Hunt (No 2) (1979)
cards.b: Where a party received a valuable non-money benefit before discharge, the court may award a just sum up to the value of that benefit. In BP v Hunt, Robert Goff J valued the benefit as the end product (oil received before Libya's expropriation), reduced by the effect of the frustrating event.

A Guns N' Roses concert was cancelled when the stadium was declared unsafe. Under s1(2) the judge has a broad discretion, and he ordered the promoters' advance to be repaid in full without deducting the defendants' expenses.

Under s2(5), the Act does not apply to voyage charterparties and other contracts for the carriage of goods by sea (time charters and demise charters are covered), insurance contracts, or contracts for the sale of specific goods frustrated by the goods perishing (including those covered by Sale of Goods Act 1979 s7). Parties can also contract out (s2(3)).

cards.f: Force majeure clauses and MUR Shipping v RTI (2024)
cards.b: Force majeure clauses are contractual and are interpreted on their wording, and the party relying on the clause must prove it applies. In MUR Shipping, the Supreme Court held that a duty to use 'reasonable endeavours' to overcome the event did not require accepting payment in a currency other than the contractual US dollars.

A failure, without lawful excuse, to perform any contractual obligation: non-performance, defective performance or repudiation. Liability is usually strict, unless the obligation is only to take reasonable care.

Breach of a condition lets the innocent party terminate and claim damages, whatever the consequences; breach of a warranty gives damages only. Poussard v Spiers (1876): a singer missing opening nights breached a condition. Bettini v Gye (1876): a singer missing some rehearsals breached a warranty.

cards.f: Hongkong Fir Shipping v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha (1962)
cards.b: The seaworthiness obligation was an innominate term. Whether the innocent party can terminate depends on how serious the breach's consequences are: does it deprive them of substantially the whole benefit of the contract? The 20 weeks lost to repairs did not, on a 24-month charter.

cards.f: How a term becomes a condition
cards.b: By statute (SGA 1979 ss12–15), by precedent, or by the parties' clear designation. Calling a term a 'condition' is not conclusive where that would be absurd: Schuler v Wickman (1974). Time clauses in mercantile contracts are usually conditions: Bunge v Tradax (1981); The Mihalis Angelos (1971).

'Shipped in good condition' was an innominate term. The buyers could not reject citrus pulp pellets that were partly damaged but still usable, and they later bought the same cargo cheaply and used it.

Arcos v Ronaasen (1933): goods that slightly departed from their description could be rejected. Now, in non-consumer sales, s15A prevents rejection for a breach of ss13–15 so slight that rejecting would be unreasonable, and the breach is treated as a breach of warranty.

A party who renounces the contract before performance is due commits an immediate breach: Hochster v De la Tour (1853). The test is whether a reasonable person in the innocent party's position would conclude the other party clearly does not intend to perform: Eminence Property Developments v Heaney (2010).

The innocent party chooses either to terminate or to affirm. Acceptance must be clear and unequivocal, but it can be by conduct, including simply not performing, if that is clearly communicated: Vitol SA v Norelf (The Santa Clara) (1996).

An innocent party may refuse a repudiation, perform, and claim the price, provided it needs no cooperation from the other side and has a legitimate interest in performing. There is no legitimate interest where damages are adequate and insisting on performance is wholly unreasonable: The Alaskan Trader (1984).
If the innocent party affirms, the contract stays alive for both parties. The original repudiator can then rely on later events, including the innocent party's own failure to perform.

Both parties' primary obligations to perform in the future are discharged. The guilty party's obligations are replaced by a secondary obligation to pay damages, including loss of bargain. Accrued rights, and clauses meant to survive (such as arbitration or exclusion clauses), remain: Photo Production (1980).

Where full performance is a condition of payment, partial performance earns nothing. Cutter v Powell (1795): a seaman died before the voyage ended, and his widow recovered nothing. Sumpter v Hedges (1898): a builder who abandoned the work could recover only for materials the owner freely chose to use.

If an entire obligation is substantially performed, the price is payable less the cost of putting defects right: Hoenig v Isaacs (1952). There was no substantial performance where defective central heating needed major work: Bolton v Mahadeva (1972).

cards.f: Time of essence and termination clauses
cards.b: Union Eagle v Golden Achievement (1997): a buyer 10 minutes late to complete lost the deposit and the contract, because time was of the essence. Lombard North Central v Butterworth (1987): a clause making punctual payment of the essence made any late payment repudiatory, so the creditor could recover loss-of-bargain damages.
The basic aim of contract damages is to put the claimant, so far as money can, in the position it would have been in if the contract had been performed. This is the expectation measure.

Wasted expenditure can be claimed instead of lost profits, including reasonably contemplated spending before the contract: Anglia Television v Reed (1972). But reliance damages cannot be used to escape a bad bargain, and the defendant may prove the venture would have made a loss: C & P Haulage v Middleton (1983); Omak Maritime v Mamola Challenger (2010).

A pool was built shallower than specified, but its value was not reduced. Rebuilding cost about £21,560, which was unreasonable and out of all proportion to the benefit, so the House of Lords upheld an award of £2,500 for loss of amenity.

Delay in delivering a broken mill shaft caused lost profits. Loss is recoverable if it arises naturally in the usual course of things (limb 1), or if both parties could reasonably have contemplated it, when contracting, as a probable result of breach (limb 2).
A boiler was delivered late. Ordinary laundry profits were recoverable, but profits from especially lucrative government dyeing contracts that the defendant did not know about were not.

cards.f: The Heron II (Koufos v C Czarnikow) (1969)
cards.b: A delayed voyage meant sugar sold into a falling market, and that loss was recoverable. The contract test requires the loss to be 'not unlikely', a serious possibility. This is stricter than the tort test of reasonable foreseeability.
If the type of loss was within reasonable contemplation, it does not matter that its extent was not. A badly ventilated nut hopper led to mouldy feed and pigs dying, and the loss was recoverable.

cards.f: Transfield Shipping v Mercator Shipping (The Achilleas) (2008)
cards.b: A vessel was redelivered late, and the owners could not recover their loss on the next fixture, only the market-rate difference for the overrun. The majority stressed whether the defendant can be taken to have assumed responsibility for that kind of loss. Later cases treat this as relevant mainly in unusual cases: Sylvia Shipping v Progress Bulk Carriers (2010).

The claimant cannot recover loss it could reasonably have avoided, and benefits gained through mitigation are deducted: British Westinghouse v Underground Electric Railways (1912). In Payzu v Saunders (1919), it was unreasonable to refuse the seller's offer to keep supplying on cash terms.

The general rule is that there are none: Addis v Gramophone (1909). They are available where a major or important object of the contract is pleasure, relaxation or peace of mind: Jarvis v Swans Tours (1973), a disappointing holiday; Farley v Skinner (2001), a surveyor who negligently reported on aircraft noise.
A beauty contest finalist was wrongly denied the chance to attend the final interview. She recovered damages for the lost chance, assessed even though it was uncertain whether she would have won.

cards.f: Penalty rule: Cavendish Square v Makdessi; ParkingEye v Beavis (2015)
cards.b: A clause triggered by breach is a penalty if it imposes a detriment out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance. 'Genuine pre-estimate of loss' (Dunlop v New Garage (1915)) is no longer the sole test. The rule applies only to obligations that arise on breach.

cards.f: Negotiating damages: Morris-Garner v One Step (Support) (2018)
cards.b: Damages measured by a hypothetical release fee are available where the breach causes the loss of a valuable asset that the contract right created or protected, such as a restrictive covenant over land (Wrotham Park Estate v Parkside Homes (1974)). They are not available where ordinary financial loss can be quantified.

An account of the defendant's profits from breach is available only in exceptional cases, where normal remedies are inadequate and the claimant has a legitimate interest in stopping the defendant profiting. The case concerned a former spy's memoir royalties.

This is an equitable, discretionary order, granted where damages are inadequate, for example for land, unique goods, or where damages would be nominal (Beswick v Beswick (1968)). It is refused for contracts of personal service, or where constant supervision would be needed: Co-operative Insurance v Argyll Stores (1998), a covenant to keep a shop open.

A promise not to work for others can be enforced by injunction: Lumley v Wagner (1852); Warner Bros v Nelson (1937), Bette Davis. It will be refused where it would in practice force the defendant to perform a personal contract: Page One Records v Britton (1968).

A claim for a debt due under the contract, such as the price, is not a claim for damages. The claimant need not prove loss, and mitigation does not apply. In sales of goods, the price can be claimed where property has passed or payment falls due on a fixed day (SGA 1979 s49).

The Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 reduces contract damages only where the defendant breached a contractual duty of care that matches a duty in tort: Forsikringsaktieselskapet Vesta v Butcher (CA, 1988). It does not apply to strict contractual obligations.

The normal date is the date of breach, but the compensatory principle lets courts take account of events after breach that reduce the true loss: The Golden Victory (2007); Bunge SA v Nidera BV (2015).

questions.q: Under English law, when a customer picks up goods from a supermarket shelf and takes them to the checkout, at what point is an offer made?
options: When the shop displays the goods on the shelf
When the customer puts the goods in the basket
When the customer presents the goods at the till
When the cashier scans the goods and states the price
questions.why: Boots Cash Chemists (1953) held that the shelf display is an invitation to treat. The customer offers at the till and the cashier accepts.

questions.q: On 1 May, A posts a letter offering to sell his car to B. On 3 May, A posts a letter revoking the offer. On 4 May, B receives the offer and immediately posts an acceptance. On 5 May, B receives the revocation. What is the legal position?
options: No contract, because the revocation was posted before the acceptance
No contract, because the acceptance was never received by A
A contract was formed on 4 May when B posted the acceptance
A contract was formed only when A received B's acceptance
questions.why: Revocation takes effect only when communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880)), whereas a posted acceptance is effective on posting (Adams v Lindsell (1818)). The acceptance therefore came first.

questions.q: State the presumptions the courts apply when deciding whether parties intended to create legal relations, giving one authority for each.
markScheme: In domestic and social agreements there is a presumption against legal intent, e.g. Balfour v Balfour (1919).
In commercial agreements there is a strong presumption in favour of legal intent, which is hard to rebut, e.g. Edwards v Skyways (1964).
questions.modelAnswer: The courts judge intention objectively and use two rebuttable presumptions. Agreements in a domestic or social setting are presumed not to be legally binding: in Balfour v Balfour (1919), a husband's promise of a monthly allowance to his wife while they lived together was not enforceable. The presumption can be displaced, for example where spouses have separated (Merritt v Merritt (1970)). Commercial agreements are presumed binding, and a party trying to rebut that bears a heavy burden: in Edwards v Skyways (1964), an 'ex gratia' payment promised to a redundant pilot was enforceable. Clear words such as an honour clause can rebut it (Rose & Frank v Crompton (1925)).

questions.q: Explain how Williams v Roffey Bros (1991) changed the law on promises to pay more for the performance of an existing contractual duty, and why the courts have refused to apply it to promises to accept less.
markScheme: Stilk v Myrick (1809): performing an existing contractual duty owed to the promisor is not consideration for a promise of extra pay.
Williams v Roffey: a promise to pay more is enforceable if the promisor obtains a practical benefit (e.g. avoiding a penalty clause) and the promise was not obtained by economic duress or fraud.

Foakes v Beer (1884), an HL decision, holds that part payment of a debt does not discharge the whole; Re Selectmove (1995) held that the Court of Appeal could not extend Roffey to this situation because of Foakes.
Evaluation: the distinction is hard to justify in principle (a creditor may get a practical benefit from prompt part payment); MWB v Rock (2018) left the question open.
questions.modelAnswer: Under Stilk v Myrick (1809), performing an existing contractual duty owed to the promisor is not good consideration for a promise of extra pay. Williams v Roffey (1991) held that such a promise is enforceable where the promisor obtains a practical benefit, such as avoiding a delay penalty or the cost of a replacement, and there is no economic duress or fraud. For promises to accept less, Foakes v Beer (1884), a House of Lords decision, binds lower courts, so in Re Selectmove (1995) the Court of Appeal refused to extend practical benefit to part payment of debts. The result is an awkward asymmetry, which the Supreme Court in MWB v Rock (2018) noted but did not resolve.

questions.q: On Monday, Priya, an antiques dealer, emailed Tom: 'I can let you have the Georgian bureau for £8,000. Offer open until Friday 5pm.' On Tuesday, Tom replied: 'Would you take £7,000? If not, I'll think about it.' Priya did not answer. On Wednesday morning, Tom's friend Lena mentioned that she had seen Priya selling the bureau to another customer. On Wednesday afternoon, Tom posted a letter to Priya saying 'I accept your offer at £8,000.' The letter arrived on Thursday. In fact, on Tuesday evening, Priya had sold the bureau to Ursula for £8,500. Advise Tom whether he has a contract with Priya.
markScheme: Identifies Priya's email as an offer: definite terms and an intention to be bound on acceptance.
A promise to keep the offer open until Friday is not binding without consideration (Routledge v Grant (1828)); Priya could revoke earlier.

Analyses Tom's reply: whether it is a counter-offer that destroys the offer (Hyde v Wrench (1840)) or a request for information/tentative inquiry (Stevenson v McLean (1880)); the words 'if not, I'll think about it' suggest he was not rejecting the £8,000 offer.
Revocation must be communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880)), but communication by a reliable third party can suffice (Dickinson v Dodds (1876)).
Discusses whether Lena's report was reliable enough; Tom would know the offer had been withdrawn if a reasonable person would rely on it.
Postal rule (Adams v Lindsell (1818)): if available, acceptance would be complete on posting on Wednesday afternoon; considers whether post was a reasonable way to reply to an email offer.
Even if the postal rule applies, the acceptance was posted after Tom learned of the sale, so revocation came first if Lena's information counts.
Remedy: if there is a contract, Tom would have a damages claim against Priya; he has no claim against Ursula, who holds good title.
Reaches a reasoned conclusion and structures the answer by stage of formation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Priya's email is an offer: it states the goods and price and shows an intention to be bound if Tom agrees. Her promise to hold it open until Friday does not bind her, because Tom gave nothing in return (Routledge v Grant (1828)). She could therefore withdraw it at any time before acceptance.

Tom's reply raises the first issue. A counter-offer rejects the original offer and destroys it (Hyde v Wrench (1840)). But 'Would you take £7,000? If not, I'll think about it' reads more like a tentative inquiry. Tom was testing whether Priya would move on price while keeping the £8,000 offer in play. As in Stevenson v McLean (1880), a reasonable offeror would not take it as a final rejection. The offer probably survived.

The second issue is revocation. Priya never told Tom herself, and revocation is only effective once communicated (Byrne v Van Tienhoven (1880)). However, Dickinson v Dodds (1876) shows that the offeree's knowledge from a reliable source is enough. Lena is a friend reporting what she saw directly. If a reasonable person would rely on her report, the offer was effectively withdrawn on Wednesday morning. If her account was vague or second-hand gossip, a court might hold that Tom did not have reliable knowledge.

The third issue is the timing of acceptance. A posted acceptance takes effect on posting where post is a reasonable means of communication (Adams v Lindsell (1818)). An offer made by email arguably invites a quick reply, so post may not have been reasonable. If the postal rule is excluded, acceptance occurs when the letter arrives on Thursday, after both the sale and Lena's report. Even if the postal rule applies, Tom posted on Wednesday afternoon, after learning of the sale that morning.

Overall, Tom is unlikely to have a contract. The decisive point is Lena's reliable report, which revoked the offer before he posted, under Dickinson v Dodds. If a court found her information unreliable and the postal rule applicable, Tom's acceptance on Wednesday afternoon would have formed a contract. His remedy would then be damages against Priya, measured by the difference between £8,000 and the market value, not recovery of the bureau from Ursula.

questions.q: BuildRight Ltd agreed to refurbish Hollis plc's office for £400,000, with completion due on 1 March and a £10,000-a-week delay penalty payable by BuildRight to Hollis. Halfway through, BuildRight's subcontractor, Cedar Joinery, said it had underpriced the work and would struggle to finish. BuildRight's manager promised Cedar an extra £30,000 if it completed on time. Cedar completed on time, but BuildRight now refuses to pay the £30,000. Separately, Hollis owed BuildRight a £100,000 stage payment. Hollis said it was short of cash, and BuildRight agreed in an email to accept £60,000 'in full and final settlement'. Hollis paid £60,000. BuildRight now claims the remaining £40,000. Advise the parties.
markScheme: Cedar: identifies the existing-duty rule in Stilk v Myrick (1809).
Applies Williams v Roffey (1991): BuildRight obtained practical benefits (avoiding the delay penalty, avoiding the cost of replacing Cedar); the promise was made voluntarily by BuildRight.
Considers economic duress: Cedar did not threaten to break the contract and its difficulty was genuine, so the pressure was not illegitimate (contrast Atlas Express v Kafco (1989)).
Notes a possible no-oral-modification clause issue (MWB v Rock (2018)) if the subcontract contains one.
Hollis: part payment of a debt is not consideration for a promise to accept less (Foakes v Beer (1884); Pinnel's Case).
Re Selectmove (1995): practical benefit cannot be used to avoid Foakes in the Court of Appeal; MWB v Rock declined to revisit it.
Checks for Pinnel exceptions (early payment, different place, extra element at the creditor's request); none apparent.
Promissory estoppel (High Trees (1947); Hughes v Metropolitan Railway (1877)): clear promise, reliance by Hollis; whether it is inequitable for BuildRight to go back.
Applies D & C Builders v Rees (1966): estoppel may fail if Hollis exploited BuildRight's position; here Hollis appears to have acted genuinely.
Discusses whether estoppel is suspensory or extinctive for a one-off debt and whether the £40,000 is permanently lost.
Evaluates the incoherence of treating promises to pay more and accept less differently.
Clear conclusion on each claim.
questions.modelAnswer:
Cedar's claim. Cedar was already bound to finish the joinery, and under Stilk v Myrick (1809) performing an existing duty owed to the promisor is not consideration. Williams v Roffey (1991), on almost identical facts, held that a promise to pay more is enforceable where (i) the promisee was already bound to perform, (ii) the promisor had reason to doubt performance, (iii) the promisor gains a practical benefit, and (iv) there was no duress or fraud. BuildRight's benefit is clear: it avoided a £10,000-a-week penalty and the disruption of replacing Cedar. On duress, Cedar did not threaten to stop work but explained a genuine difficulty, and BuildRight made the offer itself. This is unlike Atlas Express v Kafco (1989), where the carrier demanded more. Subject to any no-oral-modification clause (MWB v Rock (2018)), Cedar should recover the £30,000.

BuildRight's claim against Hollis. Foakes v Beer (1884) holds that paying part of a debt is not consideration for releasing the balance. None of the exceptions in Pinnel's Case applies: the payment was not early, not at a different place and included nothing extra. Hollis cannot rely on practical benefit, because Re Selectmove (1995) holds that Roffey does not extend to part payment while Foakes stands. At common law, BuildRight can claim the £40,000.

Hollis's best argument is promissory estoppel. BuildRight made a clear and unequivocal promise in writing, the parties had an existing contract, and Hollis relied on the promise by paying £60,000 instead of seeking other finance. The question is whether it would be inequitable for BuildRight to go back. In D & C Builders v Rees (1966), estoppel failed because the debtor exploited the creditor's cash-flow problems. Here Hollis appears to have been genuinely short of money and did not pressure BuildRight, which supports estoppel. Because estoppel is usually suspensory, BuildRight might argue it can reinstate its rights on notice. But in Collier v P & MJ Wright (Holdings) (2007), the Court of Appeal suggested, obiter, that where a creditor promises to accept part payment in settlement and the debtor pays, estoppel can extinguish the balance permanently.

Conclusion: Cedar can probably enforce the £30,000. BuildRight's £40,000 claim succeeds at common law but is likely defeated by promissory estoppel, which illustrates how hard it is to justify the difference between the 'more' and 'less' cases.

questions.q: 'The doctrine of consideration has been so weakened by practical benefit, promissory estoppel and the courts' readiness to find bargains that it no longer serves any coherent purpose. English law should openly abolish it.' Critically discuss.
markScheme: Explains the function of consideration: marking which promises are enforceable, reflecting contract as bargain/exchange, evidential and cautionary roles.
Shows the traditional rules: sufficiency not adequacy (Chappell v Nestlé (1960)); past consideration (Re McArdle (1951)); existing duties (Stilk v Myrick (1809)).
Analyses Williams v Roffey (1991) as diluting consideration, and the criticism that practical benefit is almost always present.
Discusses Foakes v Beer (1884) and Re Selectmove (1995) as creating incoherence; MWB v Rock (2018) noting the issue.
Analyses promissory estoppel (High Trees (1947)) and its limits (Combe v Combe (1951)): it supplements consideration rather than replacing it.
Notes the courts' readiness to find nominal or 'invented' consideration (e.g. Thomas v Thomas (1842); Pao On (1980)).

Considers alternatives that already exist or could replace it: deeds, economic duress as the real control on variations, intention to create legal relations, and comparative examples (civil law systems without consideration).
Weighs arguments for retention: it reflects the exchange basis of contract, limits gratuitous promises, and its dilution is targeted at variations rather than formation.
Considers law reform options (e.g. Law Revision Committee 1937 proposals) and the legislative versus judicial route.
Reaches a clear, reasoned conclusion and is well structured.
questions.modelAnswer:
Consideration is English law's test for which informal promises are enforceable. It reflects the idea that a contract is an exchange: a promise is bought by something the promisee gives or gives up (Dunlop v Selfridge (1915)). The question is whether its exceptions have hollowed it out.

There is a strong case that they have. The courts never test adequacy, so a peppercorn or used chocolate wrappers will do (Chappell v Nestlé (1960)). Where a bargain is commercially sensible, courts readily find consideration, as with the extended past consideration rule in Pao On v Lau Yiu Long (1980). Most significantly, Williams v Roffey (1991) accepted 'practical benefit' as consideration for a promise to pay more. Since almost anyone who agrees to a variation thinks it benefits them, the test is close to automatic. The real control has become economic duress, which suggests the consideration requirement no longer does the work. Meanwhile Foakes v Beer (1884) survives for promises to accept less, as Re Selectmove (1995) held, producing a distinction that critics struggle to defend. The Supreme Court in MWB v Rock (2018) admitted the area may need reconsidering. Promissory estoppel then softens Foakes in many cases (High Trees (1947)).

But the claim that consideration serves no coherent purpose overstates things. At formation, it still distinguishes bargains from gifts. A bare promise of a gift, without a deed, remains unenforceable, and estoppel cannot fill that gap, because it is a shield and not a sword (Combe v Combe (1951)). The dilution has been concentrated on variations of existing contracts, where the parties are already in an exchange relationship and the real danger is extortion, a problem better handled by duress. On that view, the modern law is coherent: consideration governs whether there is a bargain at all, while duress and estoppel police changes to it.

Abolition would also raise practical questions. Civil law systems without consideration rely on formalities for gifts instead, and English law would need an equivalent. The Law Revision Committee's 1937 proposals were never implemented, suggesting reform is for Parliament.

In conclusion, consideration has been weakened and the Roffey/Foakes split is indefensible. But it still performs a recognisable function at the formation stage. The better reform is targeted: the Supreme Court should overrule or reconcile Foakes, and duress should be the main control on variations. Open abolition would be less useful than candid rationalisation.

questions.q: Which statement best describes the modern approach to interpreting written contracts in English law?
options: The court gives effect to what each party privately intended
The court asks what the words would mean to a reasonable person with the background knowledge available to the parties
The court applies the literal dictionary meaning regardless of context
The court adopts whichever meaning it considers fairest to both parties
questions.why: Since Investors Compensation Scheme (1998), interpretation is objective and contextual: the meaning to a reasonable person with the parties' background knowledge. Arnold v Britton (2015) and Wood v Capita (2017) emphasise that the words remain central.

questions.q: A written contract is silent on a point. One party argues a term should be implied because it would make the contract fairer and more reasonable. Following Marks & Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015), how should the court respond?
options: Imply the term if a reasonable person would think it fair
Imply the term only if it is necessary for business efficacy or so obvious it goes without saying
Imply the term if one party proposed it during negotiations
Imply the term whenever the contract would otherwise be less profitable for one party
questions.why: Lord Neuberger held that reasonableness and fairness are not enough. A term is implied in fact only if it satisfies the business efficacy or the obviousness test.

questions.q: Explain the difference between terms implied in fact and terms implied in law.
markScheme: Terms implied in fact give effect to the presumed intention of the parties in a particular contract; they must be necessary for business efficacy or obvious (Marks & Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015)).
Terms implied in law are default rules attached to all contracts of a defined type, based on wider policy and necessity for that type of relationship (Liverpool CC v Irwin (1977); Scally (1992)).
Terms implied in law may also arise by statute (e.g. Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss12–15; Consumer Rights Act 2015 ss9–11), and neither type can contradict an express term.
questions.modelAnswer: Terms implied in fact fill a gap in a particular contract to reflect what the parties must have intended. Marks & Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015) sets a strict test: the term must be needed to make the contract work, or so obvious that it goes without saying. Fairness is not enough. Terms implied in law apply to every contract of a certain kind, such as landlord and tenant or employment, as a necessary incident of that relationship. They rest on broader policy, as in Liverpool CC v Irwin (1977) on common parts and Scally (1992) on telling employees about pension rights. Many are statutory, such as satisfactory quality in sales of goods. Neither kind can override clear express words.

questions.q: To what extent can evidence of pre-contractual negotiations and post-contractual conduct be used in interpreting a written contract? Briefly evaluate the rule.
markScheme: Pre-contractual negotiations are inadmissible to establish meaning (Prenn v Simmonds (1971)), confirmed in Chartbrook v Persimmon (2009).
Exceptions/qualifications: negotiations may be used to establish background facts known to both parties, and in claims for rectification or estoppel by convention.

Post-contractual conduct is inadmissible to interpret a written contract (James Miller v Whitworth Street Estates (1970)), though it may be relevant to whether a contract exists or what its terms are when it is partly oral.
Justification: negotiations show shifting positions, not agreed meaning; certainty for third parties such as assignees and lenders; litigation cost.
Criticism: excluding probative evidence may lead to meanings neither party intended; Lord Hoffmann in Chartbrook accepted the rule mainly on pragmatic grounds.
questions.modelAnswer: Prenn v Simmonds (1971) excludes evidence of negotiations to show what a contract means, and Chartbrook (2009) reaffirmed this. Negotiations may still prove a background fact known to both parties, or support rectification or estoppel by convention. Later conduct is also inadmissible to interpret a written contract (James Miller v Whitworth Street Estates (1970)), though it can show whether a contract exists or what an oral one contained. The rule is justified because negotiations record shifting positions rather than agreed meaning, third parties rely on the document alone, and costs are kept down. Critics say it can exclude the best evidence of meaning, and Lord Hoffmann in Chartbrook defended it pragmatically rather than in principle.

questions.q: Fitzgerald Gallery booked a Saturday stall at a weekend art fair run by Arcadia Events Ltd. Fitzgerald's director signed an online booking form whose first page said 'Subject to our Terms, available on request'. Clause 14 of the Terms, which was never sent to Fitzgerald, said that exhibitors who arrived after 9am would forfeit their stall and pay a 'late fee' of three times the booking price.
