Fitzgerald had booked stalls with Arcadia once before, two years earlier, using the same form. Fitzgerald arrived at 9.15am because of a road closure, was refused entry, and was invoiced for the late fee. Advise Fitzgerald on whether clause 14 is part of the contract.
markScheme: Identifies the incorporation question and the routes: signature, reasonable notice, course of dealing.

Signature rule (L'Estrange v Graucob (1934)): signing the form may bind Fitzgerald to terms referred to in it; discusses whether signing a document that refers to terms available on request incorporates them.
Reasonable notice (Parker v SE Railway (1877)): reference to terms 'available on request' can be sufficient notice in a commercial context.
Interfoto v Stiletto (1989): onerous or unusual terms require greater notice; a triple-price forfeiture plus fee is arguably onerous.
Discusses whether the Interfoto principle applies where a document is signed, noting the courts' cautious approach.
Course of dealing: one previous dealing two years earlier is unlikely to be regular and consistent (Hollier v Rambler Motors (1972); McCutcheon (1964)).
Also notes that, if incorporated, clause 14 might be challenged as a penalty under Cavendish v Makdessi (2015) and its construction considered.
Reaches a conclusion with reasons.
questions.modelAnswer:
The question is whether clause 14 was incorporated into the contract.

Signature. Under L'Estrange v Graucob (1934), a party who signs a contractual document is bound by its terms whether or not they have read them. Fitzgerald signed a form that expressly referred to the Terms. Arcadia will argue that the signature incorporated them by reference, and in commercial dealings referring to standard terms available on request is often enough. However, the signature rule binds a party most clearly to terms on the document signed. Where terms are only referred to, the court still asks whether reasonable notice of them was given.

Reasonable notice and onerous terms. Parker v South Eastern Railway (1877) requires reasonable steps to bring terms to the other party's attention before the contract is made. A reference to terms available on request may meet that standard for ordinary terms. But Interfoto v Stiletto (1989) requires that particularly onerous or unusual terms be fairly and reasonably brought to the other party's attention. Forfeiting the stall and paying three times the price for arriving fifteen minutes late is severe and unusual, much like the holding fee in Interfoto. Arcadia did nothing to highlight it. Arcadia may argue that Interfoto has less force where a document was signed, and later cases have applied the principle cautiously in signed commercial contracts. Still, because clause 14 was never sent and the form gave no hint of its content, a court is likely to find inadequate notice.

Course of dealing. A single booking two years earlier is not a regular and consistent course of dealing. In Hollier v Rambler Motors (1972), even three or four dealings over five years were insufficient, so this route fails.

Further arguments. If clause 14 were incorporated, Fitzgerald could argue the late fee is a penalty. It is a payment triggered by breach of an obligation to arrive on time, and three times the booking price looks out of all proportion to Arcadia's legitimate interest (Cavendish v Makdessi (2015)). The forfeiture element might also be read narrowly.

Conclusion: clause 14 is probably not incorporated because of Interfoto, and even if it were, the late fee is vulnerable as a penalty. Fitzgerald should refuse to pay and may claim back the booking fee or damages for being wrongly refused entry.

questions.q: Moor Holdings leased a warehouse to Gale Logistics for 15 years. The lease said: 'The Tenant shall pay an annual service charge of £20,000, increasing by 8% on each anniversary of the Term.' After 10 years, the charge had more than doubled, while the landlord's actual costs of providing services had risen only modestly. Gale argues that the parties must have meant the charge to track actual costs, or at least to rise by no more than inflation. It points to an email from Moor's agent during negotiations saying 'the uplift is just a placeholder; we can review it if costs don't keep pace'. The lease also contained a clause allowing Moor to 'determine reasonable estate regulations' which Moor has used to ban night-time deliveries, crippling Gale's business. Advise Gale.
markScheme: States the objective, contextual approach (ICS (1998); Wood v Capita (2017)).
Applies Arnold v Britton (2015): clear words govern even if the result is commercially unwise; commercial common sense cannot rewrite a bad bargain; facts are strongly analogous.
Contrasts Rainy Sky (2011): business common sense matters only where the language is genuinely ambiguous.
Considers Chartbrook correction (2009): only where something has clearly gone wrong with the language; unlikely here.

Negotiation email inadmissible to interpret (Prenn v Simmonds (1971); Chartbrook); considers its possible role in rectification, which requires a common intention outwardly expressed (FSHC v GLAS (2019)) and is unlikely on a 'placeholder' remark.
Considers implying a term capping the charge: fails Marks & Spencer v BNP (2015) because it contradicts express words and is not necessary.
Estate regulations: discretion must be exercised rationally, in good faith and not arbitrarily (Braganza v BP Shipping (2015)); also may be read to give effect to the tenant's permitted use.
Discusses whether the Braganza implied term applies to a contractual discretion of this kind and the likely outcome.
Possible derogation-from-grant or quiet enjoyment arguments noted briefly.
Structured advice with a reasoned conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
The service charge. Interpretation asks what the clause would mean to a reasonable person with the parties' background knowledge (ICS v West Bromwich (1998)). The words '£20,000, increasing by 8% on each anniversary' are clear. Arnold v Britton (2015) is closely analogous: a 10% compound increase producing very large sums was enforced. Lord Neuberger stressed that commercial common sense cannot be used to depart from clear words just because one party made a bad bargain. Rainy Sky (2011) does not help Gale, because it applies only where there are genuinely competing meanings. Nor is this a Chartbrook (2009) case where something has obviously gone wrong with the language. An 8% uplift is a coherent, if risky, bargain.

The negotiation email cannot be used to interpret the lease (Prenn v Simmonds (1971); Chartbrook). Gale's only route for it is rectification. Under FSHC v GLAS Trust (2019), Gale would have to prove a shared actual intention, outwardly expressed, that the charge would track costs, and that the lease fails to record it. A one-sided remark that the figure was 'a placeholder' to be 'reviewed' suggests an intention to renegotiate, not an agreed alternative formula, so rectification is unlikely.

An implied cap also fails. Under Marks & Spencer v BNP Paribas (2015), a term must be necessary for business efficacy or obvious, and it cannot contradict an express term. A cap would directly contradict the 8% clause.

The estate regulations. Here Gale is stronger. Where a contract gives one party a discretion that affects both parties, the courts generally imply that it must be exercised honestly, for its proper purpose, and not arbitrarily, capriciously or irrationally (Braganza v BP Shipping (2015)). The clause allows only 'reasonable' regulations, an express limit. A total ban on night deliveries for a logistics tenant, if there is no good estate-management reason, is likely to be unreasonable or irrational and outside the clause's purpose. Gale may also argue that the ban undermines the use for which the warehouse was let, raising the covenant of quiet enjoyment or non-derogation from grant.

Conclusion: Gale is bound by the service charge as written, and its email does not support rectification. It has a good argument that the delivery ban is an invalid use of Moor's discretion and should seek a declaration and, if appropriate, an injunction or damages.

questions.q: 'After Arnold v Britton and Wood v Capita, the pendulum has swung back towards literalism; Lord Hoffmann's contextual revolution is over.' Critically evaluate this statement.
markScheme: Explains Lord Hoffmann's restatement in ICS (1998): matrix of fact, 'absolutely anything' that would have affected understanding, and words read in context.
Notes the further development in Chartbrook (2009) (correcting mistakes by construction) and Rainy Sky (2011) (business common sense where ambiguity).
Analyses Arnold v Britton (2015): primacy of the words, limited role of commercial common sense, warnings against hindsight.
Analyses Wood v Capita (2017): rejects the 'swing of the pendulum' framing; textualism and contextualism are tools within one exercise.
Notes that the exclusionary rules (negotiations, later conduct) and objective approach remain unchanged.
Considers the relevance of document type: sophisticated, professionally drafted contracts versus informal ones (Wood v Capita).
Evaluates policy: certainty and predictability for commercial parties and third parties versus giving effect to real intentions.
Considers academic/judicial commentary that modern cases changed emphasis rather than principle (e.g. extrajudicial views, Lord Sumption's criticism of 'contextualism').
Assesses whether Hoffmann's approach was ever as radical as claimed, given BCCI v Ali (2001) limits.
Clear conclusion engaging directly with the quoted proposition.
questions.modelAnswer:
Lord Hoffmann's restatement in ICS v West Bromwich (1998) moved interpretation away from dictionary meanings. The court asks what the document would mean to a reasonable person with all the background knowledge reasonably available to the parties. This 'matrix of fact' could include 'absolutely anything' that would affect understanding, subject to the exclusion of negotiations and subjective intent. Chartbrook (2009) allowed courts to correct obvious errors through construction, and Rainy Sky (2011) told courts to prefer the commercially sensible meaning where the language allowed more than one.

The proposition sees Arnold v Britton (2015) as a retreat. Lord Neuberger stressed that the parties' language is central, that commercial common sense must not be used to undervalue it, and that a court cannot rescue a party from an improvident bargain. The 10% compound clause was enforced despite its harsh results. In tone this was a clear corrective to a perceived tendency to rewrite contracts in the name of context. Lord Sumption has also criticised extrajudicially how far contextualism had gone.

Yet Wood v Capita (2017) expressly rejected the 'pendulum' description. Lord Hodge said textualism and contextualism are not opposing schools but tools to be used together in a single, iterative process. How much weight each gets depends on the contract: a carefully negotiated document by skilled lawyers may be read more on its text, while an informal or badly drafted one calls for more context. On that view, Arnold changed emphasis rather than principle. The objective test, the matrix of fact and the exclusionary rules all remain. ICS itself was never meant to allow judges to ignore clear words: BCCI v Ali (2001) had already confirmed that background is limited to what a reasonable person would regard as relevant.

There is something to the proposition. Courts after Arnold are more reluctant to use commercial common sense, and Chartbrook-style correction is invoked sparingly. In practice, outcomes in professionally drafted contracts have moved towards the text. That reflects the policy value of certainty for commercial parties and for third parties such as financiers and assignees who rely on the document alone.

In conclusion, Hoffmann's revolution is not over: its core framework still governs. What has ended is a looser reading of it that let commercial common sense override clear words. 'Rebalancing' describes the change better than 'pendulum', as Wood v Capita suggests.

questions.q: Under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977, which of the following can a business NEVER exclude by a contract term in a business-to-business contract?
options: Liability for property damage caused by negligence
Liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence
Liability for late delivery
Liability for breach of the implied term as to satisfactory quality
questions.why: Section 2(1) UCTA makes exclusion of liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence wholly ineffective. The other heads are subject to the reasonableness test (ss2(2), 3, 6(1A)).

questions.q: A consumer buys a sofa from a retailer whose terms state that the sofa is sold 'as seen, with no liability for quality'. Which statement is correct?
options: The term is valid if it is reasonable under UCTA 1977
The term is binding because the consumer signed the order form
The term does not bind the consumer because the Consumer Rights Act 2015 prevents exclusion of the satisfactory quality term
The term is valid unless the consumer can prove the trader acted in bad faith
questions.why: Under CRA 2015 s31, a term excluding or restricting the s9 satisfactory quality right does not bind the consumer. UCTA no longer applies to consumer contracts.

questions.q: Outline the three-stage approach courts take when a party relies on an exemption clause.
markScheme: Incorporation: the clause must be part of the contract (signature, reasonable notice, course of dealing).
Construction: the clause must, properly interpreted, cover the loss (contra proferentem, Canada Steamship guidelines for negligence, Photo Production (1980)).
Statutory control: the clause must survive UCTA 1977 (non-consumer) or the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (consumer).
questions.modelAnswer: First, the clause must be incorporated, whether by signature (L'Estrange v Graucob (1934)), by reasonable notice given before or at the time of contracting (Olley v Marlborough Court (1949)), or by a consistent course of dealing. Second, on its proper construction it must cover the breach and loss in question. Ambiguity is read against the party relying on the clause, and clear words are needed to exclude negligence (Canada Steamship (1952)), though Photo Production (1980) confirms there is no rule of law preventing exclusion of serious breaches. Third, it must survive statute: UCTA 1977 for business contracts, or Part 2 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 for consumer contracts.

questions.q: Explain how the 'core terms' exemption in s64 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 operates, and why it matters.
markScheme: s64 excludes from the fairness assessment terms specifying the main subject matter or the appropriateness of the price compared with goods/services supplied.
The exemption applies only if the term is transparent (plain, intelligible and, if written, legible) and prominent (brought to the average consumer's attention).
Terms on the grey list in Sch 2 Part 1 cannot benefit from the exemption (s64(6)).
Significance: it prevents courts reviewing the fairness of the bargain itself (cf. OFT v Abbey National (2009) on bank charges) while requiring openness; the 2015 Act tightened the position.
questions.modelAnswer: Section 64 removes from fairness review terms defining the main subject matter, or concerning whether the price is appropriate for what is supplied, because consumers can judge the core bargain themselves and courts should not set prices. The exemption applies only if the term is transparent (plain, intelligible and legible) and prominent (brought to the average consumer's attention). Grey-list terms in Schedule 2 Part 1 can never be exempt. This matters because in OFT v Abbey National (2009), overdraft charges escaped review as price terms under the earlier regulations. The prominence requirement makes it harder for traders to bury charges in small print and still claim the exemption.

questions.q: Agri-Tech Ltd, a large supplier, sold specialised irrigation software to Harrow Farms Ltd, a family-run farming company, for £15,000 on Agri-Tech's standard terms, which Harrow signed without negotiation. Clause 9 provided: 'Seller's total liability for any loss, howsoever arising, is limited to the price paid. Seller shall not be liable for any loss of crops or profits.' A bug in the software, which Agri-Tech's engineers had known about but not fixed, caused the irrigation system to fail during a heatwave. Harrow lost crops worth £240,000. Agri-Tech carries product liability insurance of £5 million. Advise Harrow.
markScheme: Incorporation: clause signed, so incorporated (L'Estrange v Graucob (1934)).

Construction: 'howsoever arising' and express exclusion of crop loss likely cover the loss; limitation clauses construed less strictly (Ailsa Craig (1983)); considers Canada Steamship and whether negligence is covered.
UCTA applies because this is a business-to-business contract; identifies s3 (written standard terms) and s6(1A)/s2(2) as relevant controls.
Notes the uncertainty over whether software supplied in this way counts as 'goods' for s6; s3 applies regardless.
Reasonableness test: s11(1) at time of contract; burden on Agri-Tech (s11(5)).
Applies Sch 2 guidelines: unequal bargaining power, no negotiation, no alternative offered.
s11(4): availability of insurance and resources relevant to limitation clauses; Agri-Tech insured.
Uses George Mitchell v Finney Lock (1983) and contrasts Watford Electronics v Sanderson (2001).
Conclusion: clause likely unreasonable; Harrow recovers £240,000 subject to remoteness and mitigation.
questions.modelAnswer:
Incorporation. Harrow signed Agri-Tech's terms, so clause 9 is incorporated (L'Estrange v Graucob (1934)).

Construction. Clause 9 has two parts: a cap at the price paid, and an exclusion of crop loss and lost profits. Limitation clauses are read less strictly than total exclusions (Ailsa Craig (1983)). The words 'howsoever arising' and the express reference to crop loss probably cover the failure. Agri-Tech's liability for breach of the implied terms is strict, so under the third Canada Steamship guideline there is a realistic non-negligence head the words could cover. But those guidelines are only aids to construction, they apply less strictly to limitation clauses, and 'howsoever arising' is wide enough to be read as including negligence in not fixing a known bug. Under the modern approach (Triple Point v PTT (2021)), clear words are needed to remove valuable rights, but these words are fairly clear.

Statutory control. This is a business-to-business contract, so UCTA 1977 applies. Harrow dealt on Agri-Tech's written standard terms, so s3 subjects the clause to the reasonableness test. If the software counts as goods, which is uncertain for software, s6(1A) also applies to the implied terms on quality and fitness. If negligence caused the loss, s2(2) applies. Under every route, the clause must be reasonable, judged at the time of contracting (s11(1)), and Agri-Tech bears the burden of proof (s11(5)).

Reasonableness. Under the Schedule 2 guidelines, the parties had very unequal bargaining power: a large supplier and a family farm. The terms were standard and not negotiated, and nothing suggests Harrow was offered a higher price for wider cover. For limitation clauses, s11(4) points to Agri-Tech's resources and its ability to insure. It holds £5 million cover. In George Mitchell v Finney Lock Seeds (1983), limiting liability for defective seed to its price was unreasonable where the seller could insure and the buyer could not guard against a hidden defect. These facts are similar: Harrow could not detect the bug, while Agri-Tech knew about it. Agri-Tech will cite Watford Electronics v Sanderson (2001), but that involved experienced parties of comparable strength negotiating terms, unlike here.

Conclusion. A court is likely to find clause 9 unreasonable, so it will not apply. Harrow can claim damages for its crop loss. Agri-Tech may still argue remoteness, but failed irrigation leading to lost crops is a natural consequence (Hadley v Baxendale, limb 1). Mitigation will also be considered.

questions.q: Zara, a consumer, joined FitLife gym on a 24-month membership at £50 a month. FitLife's online terms, accepted by ticking a box, included: (a) 'If you cancel within the minimum term, you must pay all remaining monthly fees immediately.' (b) 'FitLife may change monthly fees at any time on 7 days' notice.' (c) 'FitLife accepts no liability for injury on the premises, however caused.' After three months, Zara was injured when a poorly maintained treadmill collapsed. She then lost her job and wants to cancel. FitLife has increased the fee to £70 and demands £1,470 in remaining fees. Advise Zara under the Consumer Rights Act 2015.
markScheme: Identifies the contract as a trader–consumer contract within Part 2 CRA 2015 (s61); UCTA does not apply.
Clause (c): s65 – liability for death or personal injury resulting from negligence cannot be excluded; also s57 (services with reasonable care and skill, s49) cannot be excluded.
Clause (a): considers whether it is a core price term exempt under s64 – requires transparency and prominence; likely fails or is grey-listed.

Applies s62 fairness test: good faith, significant imbalance, detriment (DGFT v First National Bank (2001)); grey-list terms in Sch 2 Part 1 on disproportionate compensation and retention of sums paid.
Discusses legitimate interest and whether accelerating all fees is disproportionate given FitLife's ability to re-let capacity; may also be a penalty (Cavendish/ParkingEye (2015)).
Contrasts ParkingEye v Beavis (2015) where a charge was upheld as justified by a legitimate interest.
Clause (b): unilateral variation of price without valid reason or right to cancel – grey-list terms in Sch 2 Part 1 on unilateral variation of terms and price; likely unfair.
Effect of unfairness: term not binding on consumer, contract continues so far as practicable (s67); court must consider fairness of its own motion (s71).
Enforcement: CMA and regulators can act (s70, Sch 3).
Reasoned conclusion on each clause and Zara's position.
questions.modelAnswer:
Zara is a consumer contracting with a trader, so Part 2 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 applies, and the court must consider fairness even if she does not raise it (s71).

Clause (c): injury. This is blacklisted. Under s65, a trader cannot exclude or restrict liability for death or personal injury caused by negligence. Section 57 also prevents exclusion of the duty to perform services with reasonable care and skill (s49). Clause (c) has no effect, and Zara can claim damages for her injury.

Clause (a): accelerated fees. FitLife may argue this is a core term about price and exempt under s64. But it governs early termination, not the main service or price. Even if it could qualify, the exemption needs the term to be transparent and prominent. A clause buried in tick-box terms is unlikely to be prominent enough. The term is therefore assessed under s62: is it contrary to good faith, and does it cause a significant imbalance to Zara's detriment? Lord Bingham in First National Bank (2001) linked good faith to fair and open dealing. The Schedule 2 grey list includes terms requiring a consumer who fails to perform to pay disproportionately high compensation, and terms letting the trader keep sums the consumer has paid when the consumer cancels. Demanding all 21 months' fees at once, with no deduction for FitLife's saved costs or ability to re-sell the place, looks disproportionate. FitLife may rely on ParkingEye v Beavis (2015), where a charge was upheld because it protected a legitimate interest. A reasonable early termination fee might pass, but full acceleration is likely unfair. It may also be attacked as a penalty under Cavendish (2015).

Clause (b): price variation. A term allowing the trader to change the price without a valid reason specified in the contract, and without letting the consumer cancel, is grey-listed in Schedule 2. With no right to leave, it is likely unfair.

Effect. Unfair terms do not bind the consumer, but the rest of the contract continues where practicable (s67). Zara is not bound by clauses (a), (b) or (c). If she cancels, FitLife cannot rely on the acceleration clause. Its claim would be at most for damages for her breach, subject to its duty to mitigate. She can claim for her injury. Zara could also complain to the CMA, which has enforcement powers (s70 and Sch 3).

questions.q: 'The reasonableness test under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 gives judges too much discretion and too little guidance, producing unpredictable outcomes in commercial contracts. Parliament should leave businesses free to allocate risk as they see fit.' Discuss.
markScheme: Explains the scope of UCTA after 2015: business liability in non-consumer contracts, ss2, 3, 6 and 7; s3 MA 1967.
Describes the reasonableness test: s11, burden on the party relying on the clause, Sch 2 guidelines, s11(4) on limitation clauses.
Analyses appellate restraint: George Mitchell v Finney Lock (1983) (appellate courts should not interfere unless plainly wrong).
Discusses the trend of deference to commercial parties: Watford Electronics (2001); Granville Oil & Chemicals v Davis Turner (2003); also Goodlife Foods v Hall Fire Protection (2018).
Contrasts cases striking clauses down: Stewart Gill v Horatio Myer (1992); St Albans v ICL (1996); Smith v Eric S Bush (1990).
Evaluates predictability: fact-sensitive approach, time of contracting, factors well-established; but inconsistent outcomes.
Freedom of contract arguments: insurance allocation, pricing, efficiency, the parties as best judges; small businesses may lack bargaining power.
Considers whether UCTA is justified as protection for weaker businesses (SMEs), and alternative approaches (e.g. thresholds, CRA-style protection for micro-businesses, comparative models).
Notes that some protections are absolute (s2(1), s6(1)) and the case for retaining them.
Reaches a balanced conclusion directly addressing both limbs of the proposition.
questions.modelAnswer:
Since 2015, UCTA has applied mainly to business-to-business contracts. Some protections are absolute: liability for negligently caused death or personal injury (s2(1)) and for the implied term about title (s6(1)) cannot be excluded. Most others are subject to the reasonableness test. Under s11, a term must be fair and reasonable given the circumstances known or contemplated when the contract was made. The party relying on the term bears the burden (s11(5)). Schedule 2's guidelines and s11(4)'s factors on resources and insurance shape the inquiry.

The criticism of excessive discretion has some force. Reasonableness is open-textured and depends on the facts, and the House of Lords in George Mitchell v Finney Lock (1983) told appellate courts not to interfere unless the judge was plainly wrong. That means similar clauses can be treated differently by different trial judges. Early decisions striking down clauses, such as Stewart Gill v Horatio Myer (1992) and St Albans DC v ICL (1996), unsettled commercial expectations.

However, the modern case law offers more guidance and more deference than the proposition suggests. Watford Electronics v Sanderson (2001) held that experienced businesses of equal bargaining power are the best judges of commercial fairness, and courts should be slow to interfere. Granville Oil & Chemicals v Davis Turner (2003) followed this approach for standard trade terms. Goodlife Foods v Hall Fire Protection (2018) upheld a limitation clause where the customer could have insured or negotiated a higher price for more cover. Clauses are most at risk where there is real inequality, no negotiation, no alternative offered, or where the party relying on the clause could easily insure. In negotiated contracts between sophisticated parties, the test rarely bites.

The freedom-of-contract argument is that businesses price risk and insure against it, and that striking out limitation clauses makes risk allocation inefficient. That argument is strongest for large commercial parties. It is weaker for small businesses, which often contract on non-negotiable standard terms with the same lack of bargaining power as consumers. Abolishing UCTA would leave such businesses unprotected, with only incorporation and construction rules to help.

A targeted reform would be better, such as exempting large negotiated contracts while giving micro-businesses stronger protection. In conclusion, the test involves discretion, but appellate deference and the Watford line have made it reasonably predictable for commercial parties, and it still protects weaker businesses. Rather than abolition, Parliament should calibrate it more clearly.

questions.q: What is the effect of a misrepresentation on a contract it induced?
options: The contract is void from the start
The contract is voidable, so the misled party may rescind it
The contract is automatically terminated for breach
The contract is valid, and the only remedy is an apology
questions.why: Misrepresentation makes the contract voidable. The misled party may elect to rescind, subject to the bars, and may also be entitled to damages.

questions.q: A seller of a restaurant tells a buyer it 'currently turns over £5,000 a week'. This was true when said, but turnover falls to £2,000 a week before contracts are exchanged three months later, and the seller says nothing. Which authority best supports the buyer's claim?
options: Bisset v Wilkinson (1927)
With v O'Flanagan (1936)
Keates v Cadogan (1851)
Smith v Hughes (1871)
questions.why: With v O'Flanagan holds that a statement which becomes false before the contract is concluded must be corrected; failing to do so is a misrepresentation.

questions.q: A rogue visits a jeweller, claims to be a well-known actor, and pays for a ring with a cheque that bounces. Before the jeweller discovers the fraud, the rogue sells the ring to an innocent buyer. Applying current authority, what is the most likely outcome?
options: The contract is void for mistaken identity, so the innocent buyer gets no title
The contract is voidable for fraud but was not rescinded before the resale, so the innocent buyer gets good title
The contract is void because the cheque bounced
The innocent buyer must return the ring because the jeweller never intended to sell
questions.why: In face-to-face dealings, the seller is presumed to intend to deal with the person present (Phillips v Brooks (1919); Lewis v Averay (1972); Shogun Finance (2003)). The contract is voidable, and a buyer in good faith before rescission takes good title.

questions.q: Compare the damages available for fraudulent misrepresentation and for misrepresentation under s2(1) of the Misrepresentation Act 1967.
markScheme: Fraud (Derry v Peek (1889)): claimant must prove the defendant knew the statement was false, had no belief in it, or was reckless; heavy burden.
Damages for deceit cover all loss directly flowing, foreseeable or not (Doyle v Olby (1969); Smith New Court (1997)).
s2(1): burden reversed – defendant liable unless they prove reasonable grounds for belief up to the time of contracting (Howard Marine v Ogden (1978)).
Royscot Trust v Rogerson (1991): s2(1) damages assessed on the fraud measure ('fiction of fraud'), though criticised and doubted in Smith New Court.
questions.modelAnswer: For fraud, the claimant must prove the defendant knew the statement was false, did not believe it, or was reckless (Derry v Peek (1889)), which is hard to establish. Damages in deceit then cover all loss flowing directly from the fraud, even if unforeseeable (Doyle v Olby (1969); Smith New Court (1997)). Under s2(1), the claimant need only prove a false statement that induced the contract. The defendant is liable unless it proves it reasonably believed the statement true up to the contract, which the defendant failed to do in Howard Marine v Ogden (1978). Royscot Trust v Rogerson (1991) measures s2(1) damages as if for fraud, though this was doubted in Smith New Court.

questions.q: Explain the approach to common mistake in Great Peace Shipping v Tsavliris Salvage (2002) and evaluate whether it is preferable to the equitable jurisdiction recognised in Solle v Butcher (1950).
markScheme: Great Peace requirements: a common assumption about a state of affairs; no warranty by either party that it exists; non-existence not attributable to either party's fault; non-existence renders performance impossible/essentially different; the state of affairs must be the vital attribute.
Applied on the facts: the vessel was 410 miles away rather than 35, but the contract could still be performed meaningfully, so not void.
Built on Bell v Lever Bros (1932) and McRae (1951).
Rejected Solle v Butcher's separate equitable power to rescind for a 'fundamental' mistake as inconsistent with Bell.

Evaluation: gains certainty and respects risk allocation; loses flexibility (Solle allowed terms to be imposed); the narrowness may be acceptable given contractual risk allocation and the availability of other doctrines.
questions.modelAnswer: In Great Peace (2002), the Court of Appeal held that a contract is void for common mistake only where both parties shared an assumption about a state of affairs, neither warranted it, neither was at fault for its absence, and its absence made performance essentially different from what they contemplated. This follows Bell v Lever Bros (1932). The vessel was further away than believed, but the hire could still be performed, so the contract stood. Solle v Butcher's wider equitable power to rescind was held inconsistent with Bell. The approach gains certainty and respects risk allocation, but loses Solle's flexibility to rescind on terms. Since parties can allocate risk expressly, the stricter rule is defensible.

questions.q: Dev wanted to buy a second-hand delivery van for his new courier business. At Speedy Motors, a dealer, the salesperson Keira told him: 'This van has done 40,000 miles, and it's in great nick. It'll easily do the job.' Dev bought it for £18,000 the next day. Two weeks later, a mechanic told Dev the true mileage was about 110,000 miles and that the odometer had been wound back before Speedy bought it at auction. Keira had not checked the van's service history, which was in a folder in the office and showed the higher mileage. Dev has continued to use the van for his deliveries while deciding what to do. Advise Dev on his remedies for misrepresentation.
markScheme: Identifies the mileage statement as a false statement of existing fact; 'great nick' and 'easily do the job' as possible opinion, but from a dealer with superior knowledge implying facts (Smith v Land & House (1884); contrast Bisset v Wilkinson (1927)).
Inducement: the statement was material and likely induced the purchase; no duty to check (Redgrave v Hurd (1881)).
Considers whether the statement became a term (Dick Bentley v Harold Smith (1965)) enabling contractual damages.
Fraud unlikely: Keira honestly believed it; carelessness is not fraud (Derry v Peek (1889)).
s2(1) MA 1967: Speedy must prove reasonable grounds for belief; failure to check available service history suggests not (Howard Marine v Ogden (1978)).
Damages under s2(1) on the fraud measure (Royscot (1991)), covering losses directly flowing.
Rescission: available but bars – affirmation by continued use after discovery (Long v Lloyd (1958)), lapse of time; Dev should act promptly.
s2(2): court may award damages instead of rescission for non-fraudulent misrepresentation.
Concludes with practical advice.
questions.modelAnswer:
Actionable misrepresentation. 'This van has done 40,000 miles' is a statement of existing fact, and it was false. 'In great nick' and 'it'll easily do the job' sound like opinion. But a dealer has superior knowledge, so the statements imply that Keira knew facts justifying them (Smith v Land & House (1884)). Bisset v Wilkinson (1927), where neither party had better knowledge, can be distinguished. The mileage is plainly material to a buyer who needs a working van, so inducement can be inferred. Dev did not need to check the history himself (Redgrave v Hurd (1881)).

Term or representation? Because Speedy is a dealer, the mileage statement may well be a contractual term, as in Dick Bentley v Harold Smith (1965), where a dealer's mileage statement was treated as a warranty. If so, Dev can also claim damages for breach. Since Speedy deals in vehicles, the Consumer Rights Act 2015 may also apply if Dev bought as a consumer, but he is buying for his business, so the Sale of Goods Act 1979 is more likely to govern.

Fraud? Keira seems to have honestly believed the mileage, so fraud is unlikely. Carelessness, even gross carelessness, is not fraud (Derry v Peek (1889)).

Section 2(1) Misrepresentation Act 1967. This is Dev's best route. Speedy is liable unless it proves it had reasonable grounds to believe, and did believe, the statement up to the time of contract. The service history showing higher mileage was in its own office. Like the owners in Howard Marine v Ogden (1978), who failed to check reliable documents they had, Speedy is unlikely to discharge the burden. Damages are assessed on the fraud measure (Royscot Trust v Rogerson (1991)). Dev can recover the difference between the £18,000 price and the van's true value, plus consequential losses flowing directly from the purchase, such as repair costs.

Rescission. Dev could rescind and return the van for a refund, but there are bars. Continuing to use it after discovering the truth may count as affirmation (Long v Lloyd (1958)), and delay can bar relief. Dev should stop using the van and notify Speedy promptly. Even if rescission remains available, the court has discretion under s2(2) to award damages instead.

Advice: Dev should give notice of rescission immediately and, in the alternative, claim damages under s2(1) and, if the mileage was a term, for breach of contract.

questions.q: Mirela, aged 72, lives with her nephew Ollie, who manages her finances and drives her to appointments. Ollie runs a struggling café. At his suggestion, Mirela agreed to charge her house, worth £600,000, to Northern Bank as security for a £250,000 business loan to Ollie's company. The bank sent the documents to Ollie, who brought them home. He told Mirela the charge was 'just a formality – they'd never take the house'. A solicitor, instructed by the bank and also acting for Ollie's company, met Mirela for ten minutes and signed a certificate saying he had explained the documents. The café has failed, and the bank seeks possession. Separately, Ollie's supplier, Vend Co, had forced Ollie to sign a price increase by threatening to stop deliveries during the café's busiest week, knowing it had no contractual right to do so. Advise Mirela and Ollie.
markScheme: Undue influence categories after Etridge (2001): actual and presumed; relationship of trust and confidence plus a transaction calling for explanation.
Applies: Ollie manages Mirela's finances – relationship of trust and confidence likely; charging her home for his business debt calls for explanation.
Also misrepresentation by Ollie ('just a formality').
Bank's position: put on inquiry because the relationship is non-commercial and she is a surety (Etridge).

Etridge steps: bank should communicate directly with the surety, obtain confirmation from a solicitor acting for her, and give the solicitor necessary financial information; the solicitor should meet face to face without the debtor present and explain core points.

Assesses whether the bank took reasonable steps: certificate from a solicitor who also acted for the debtor company; short meeting; Ollie delivering documents – arguably insufficient; solicitor may act for both if he considers it in her interest, but quality of advice matters.
Consequence: if the bank is fixed with notice, the charge may be set aside against Mirela; she may also have a claim against the solicitor.

Ollie and Vend: economic duress – illegitimate pressure (threat to breach contract, known to be without right) that was a significant cause (Universe Tankships (1983); DSND (2000); Atlas Express v Kafco (1989)).
Practical alternative: lack of reasonable alternative during busiest week; protest and prompt action to avoid affirmation (North Ocean Shipping v Hyundai (The Atlantic Baron) (1979)).
Remedy: rescission of the price variation and recovery of any excess paid; conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mirela and Northern Bank. Under RBS v Etridge (No 2) (2001), undue influence may be actual or presumed. Ollie manages Mirela's finances and she depends on him, so she is likely to show a relationship of trust and confidence. Charging her home, her main asset, to secure his company's debt is a transaction that calls for explanation, so influence is presumed unless Ollie shows she acted freely. Ollie also misrepresented the effect of the charge by calling it 'just a formality'.

The key question is whether the bank is affected. Etridge holds that a lender is put on inquiry whenever a person stands surety for another's debts in a non-commercial relationship. Aunt and nephew qualify. The bank is protected only if it took reasonable steps to ensure Mirela understood the transaction. These include communicating directly with her, getting confirmation from a solicitor acting for her that she had been advised, and giving that solicitor the financial information needed. The solicitor should advise her face to face, without the debtor present.

Here the bank sent documents through Ollie, which is exactly what Etridge warns against. The solicitor also acted for Ollie's company. Etridge allows one solicitor to act for both sides if he considers this compatible with his duties, but a ten-minute meeting is unlikely to cover the core points properly. Reliance on the certificate is weakened because the bank communicated through Ollie, not directly. A court could well find the bank did not take reasonable steps and has constructive notice. The charge would then be set aside against Mirela. She may also sue the solicitor in negligence.

Ollie and Vend Co. Economic duress requires illegitimate pressure that was a significant cause of the agreement (Universe Tankships (1983); DSND Subsea (2000)). A threat to breach a contract, made knowing there was no right to do so, is classic illegitimate pressure (Atlas Express v Kafco (1989)). Ollie had no practical alternative during his busiest week, which supports causation. To avoid losing the right to rescind, he must protest and act promptly. In The Atlantic Baron (1979), delay amounted to affirmation. If he does, he can rescind the price increase and recover any excess paid.

Conclusion: Mirela has a strong argument to set aside the charge, and Ollie can avoid the price increase if he acts without delay.

questions.q: 'English law's treatment of mistaken identity, culminating in Shogun Finance v Hudson, turns on an arbitrary distinction between written and face-to-face dealings and unjustly sacrifices innocent purchasers.' Critically evaluate this claim and consider how the law should be reformed.
markScheme: Explains the distinction: written contracts identifying a party (Cundy v Lindsay (1878); Shogun (2003)) versus face-to-face presumption (Phillips v Brooks (1919); Lewis v Averay (1972); contrast Ingram v Little (1961)).

Explains consequences: void contract means no title passes to an innocent third party; voidable contract means title passes if no rescission before resale (cf. Car & Universal Finance v Caldwell (1965)).
Analyses Shogun majority reasoning: construction of the written agreement identifying the hirer; parol evidence; Hire Purchase Act 1964 context.
Analyses minority (Lords Nicholls and Millett): would have overruled Cundy and applied a single presumption in favour of a voidable contract to protect third parties.
Evaluates arbitrariness: the rogue's fraud is the same; the medium of contracting decides who bears loss; modern remote and online dealings make the distinction more important.
Considers policy: which of two innocent parties should bear the loss; the original owner may be better placed to guard against fraud; security of transactions.

Considers reform options: Law Reform Committee's 12th Report (1966) recommended that such contracts be voidable not void; apportionment of loss between innocent parties (Devlin LJ in Ingram v Little); nemo dat exceptions.
Notes statutory exceptions (Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss21–25; Hire Purchase Act 1964 Part III).
Reaches a reasoned conclusion with a preferred reform.
questions.modelAnswer:
Mistaken identity decides which of two innocent parties bears a rogue's fraud. If the contract is void, no title passes and the owner can recover the goods from an innocent purchaser; if it is voidable, a good-faith buyer before rescission keeps them.

The current law turns largely on how the parties dealt. Where the contract is in writing and identifies a specific person, the courts treat the named person as the only intended party. In Cundy v Lindsay (1878), a rogue imitating a reputable firm's name obtained no contract. In Shogun Finance v Hudson (2003), a rogue took a car on hire purchase using another man's stolen identity; the majority held the written agreement was with that man alone, so it was void and the innocent buyer got no title under the Hire Purchase Act 1964. By contrast, in face-to-face dealings there is a strong presumption that the seller intends to deal with the person physically present (Phillips v Brooks (1919); Lewis v Averay (1972)), so the contract is merely voidable.

The claim of arbitrariness is powerful. The fraud is the same whether committed in person, by letter or online, yet the medium decides who keeps the goods. The Shogun minority, Lords Nicholls and Millett, would have overruled Cundy and held such contracts voidable, not void. Online dealing makes the written-contract rule ever more significant.

The majority's defence is principled in its own terms. Interpretation is objective, and where a written document identifies the parties, a court should not rewrite it. But the result is hard to justify on policy grounds: the owner chose to deal with an unverified person and is better placed to guard against fraud.

On reform, the Law Reform Committee's 12th Report (1966) recommended that such contracts be voidable, not void, so that innocent purchasers are protected. Devlin LJ's dissent in Ingram v Little (1961) suggested splitting the loss between innocent parties. That is fairer but would make outcomes less certain. A further option is to widen the statutory exceptions to nemo dat in the Sale of Goods Act 1979 ss21–25.

In conclusion, the distinction is largely arbitrary in its effects and favours owners over purchasers without strong justification. The preferable reform is a legislative rule that identity mistakes induced by fraud make a contract voidable only. That would align English law with the Shogun minority's single presumption.

questions.q: Which of the following is the leading statement of the test for frustration in English law?
options: Performance has become more expensive than either party expected
Without either party's fault, performance has become radically different from what was undertaken
One party can no longer make a profit from the contract
A party has given reasonable notice that it no longer wishes to perform
questions.why: Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC (1956) frames frustration as a supervening event that makes performance radically different, not merely more onerous or expensive.

questions.q: A seller agrees to sell goods CIF Hamburg, to be shipped from Port Sudan. The usual route through the Suez Canal is closed, and the voyage around the Cape takes twice as long and costs considerably more. Following Tsakiroglou v Noblee Thorl (1962), what is the likely outcome?
options: The contract is frustrated because the agreed route is unavailable
The contract is frustrated because the cost has doubled
The contract is not frustrated because performance by another route is not radically different
The contract is void for common mistake
questions.why: In Tsakiroglou, the House of Lords held that shipping via the Cape, though longer and more expensive, was not fundamentally different performance, so the contract was not frustrated.

questions.q: Explain the effect of frustration at common law, and why the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 was passed.
markScheme: Frustration automatically discharges the contract from the moment of the event; future obligations end and accrued obligations remain (Chandler v Webster (1904)).
Fibrosa (1943) allowed recovery of money paid where there was a total failure of consideration, but not partial failure, and gave the payee nothing for expenses.
The 1943 Act allows recovery of money paid and relief from money payable (s1(2)), a discretionary allowance for expenses, and a just sum for valuable non-money benefits (s1(3)).
questions.modelAnswer: At common law, frustration ends the contract automatically from the moment of the event, without either party electing to terminate. Obligations that have already accrued remain enforceable, while future obligations are discharged (Chandler v Webster (1904)). Fibrosa (1943) softened Chandler by allowing recovery of a prepayment where consideration had failed totally. But it gave no remedy for partial failure and nothing for the payee's expenses. The 1943 Act addressed these gaps. Section 1(2) allows money paid to be recovered and money payable to be cancelled, with a discretionary allowance for the payee's expenses. Section 1(3) allows the court to award a just sum for valuable benefits other than money conferred before discharge.

questions.q: Explain how the court values a claim under s1(3) of the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943, with reference to BP Exploration v Hunt (No 2) (1979), and identify one criticism of that approach.
markScheme: s1(3): where a party has obtained a valuable benefit (other than money) before discharge, the court may award a just sum not exceeding the value of the benefit.
Robert Goff J: first identify and value the benefit, then assess the just sum up to that cap.
The 'benefit' is the end product received (the oil and its value), not the value of the services performed.
s1(3)(b): the value must take account of the effect of the frustrating event on the benefit (the expropriation reduced it).

Criticism: if the frustrating event destroys the end product (e.g. a building burns down), the benefit may be nil and the performing party recovers nothing, as illustrated by Appleby v Myers (1867)-type facts; or the approach ignores the cost of the services.
questions.modelAnswer: Section 1(3) allows a just sum where one party received a valuable non-money benefit before frustration, capped at the benefit's value. In BP v Hunt (No 2) (1979), Robert Goff J first identified and valued the benefit, treating it as the end product of BP's work (the oil Hunt received and his enhanced concession) rather than the work itself. Under s1(3)(b), he took account of how the frustrating event, Libya's expropriation, reduced it. He then assessed a just sum within that cap. The main criticism is that where the frustrating event destroys the end product, such as a partly built structure that burns down, the benefit may be nil and a party who did much work recovers nothing.

questions.q: Lumen Events Ltd hired the Riverside Pavilion from Hartley Venues for a three-day music festival from 10 to 12 July, for a fee of £90,000. Lumen paid £30,000 on signing, with the balance due on 1 July. The contract contained no force majeure clause. Lumen spent £20,000 on advertising and staging. On 25 June, the local authority closed the Pavilion indefinitely after inspectors found serious structural defects that neither party had known about. Hartley had spent £8,000 preparing the site for the festival. Advise the parties on whether the contract is frustrated and, if so, the financial consequences.
markScheme: States the frustration test (Davis Contractors (1956)); analogy with Taylor v Caldwell (1863) – venue unavailable.
Checks that the event was not caused by either party (self-induced frustration) and not provided for or foreseen and allocated by the contract.

Considers whether Hartley assumed the risk of the structural defects (it owned the venue); discusses the possibility that the risk was implicitly allocated to Hartley, and The Sea Angel (2007) multi-factorial approach.
Concludes the contract is likely frustrated: performance impossible, not merely more onerous.
Common law effect: discharge from 25 June; Chandler v Webster/Fibrosa background.
1943 Act s1(2): Lumen recovers the £30,000 paid; the £60,000 balance, not due until 1 July (after discharge), simply falls away and does not count towards the expenses cap.
Expenses proviso: court may let Hartley retain up to £8,000 of the £30,000 if just (Gamerco v ICM (1995) – broad discretion; may refuse).
Lumen's £20,000 spending is not recoverable from Hartley under the Act (no benefit conferred on Hartley); notes s1(3) does not assist.
Structured conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
Is the contract frustrated? Frustration occurs when, without either party's fault, an event makes performance radically different from what was undertaken (Davis Contractors (1956)). The facts closely resemble Taylor v Caldwell (1863), where the hall burned down before the concerts. Here the Pavilion has been closed indefinitely by the authorities, so the festival cannot take place there. This is impossibility, not just extra cost.

Two limits must be checked. First, the event must not be self-induced. Neither party knew of the defects, and the closure was imposed by the authority, so it was not caused by either party's choice (contrast Maritime National Fish (1935)). Lumen might argue that Hartley, as owner, should bear responsibility for its building's condition. If Hartley had been negligent in not discovering defects it should have found, it might be treated as at fault or as having warranted the venue's fitness, in which case Lumen would claim damages instead. Second, the contract has no force majeure clause and nothing suggests the parties foresaw and allocated this risk. Applying the multi-factorial approach in The Sea Angel (2007), and assuming Hartley was not at fault, the contract is likely frustrated on 25 June.

Consequences. At common law, the contract ends automatically on 25 June. The 1943 Act then governs the money. Under s1(2), Lumen can recover the £30,000 it paid. The £60,000 balance was not due until 1 July, after discharge, so it falls away with the other future obligations and is not 'payable' before discharge for the purposes of the expenses cap. Hartley may ask the court to let it keep part of the £30,000 to cover its £8,000 of expenses incurred in performing. This is discretionary and must be 'just'. In Gamerco v ICM (1995), the judge used his broad discretion to order full repayment without deduction, reasoning that both parties had lost out. A court might allow Hartley some or all of the £8,000, or might decline because Lumen has also lost heavily.

Lumen's own £20,000 spending on advertising and staging cannot be recovered from Hartley. The Act's expenses provision protects only the payee. Section 1(3) does not help either, because Lumen's spending conferred no valuable benefit on Hartley.

Conclusion: the contract is likely frustrated. Lumen recovers £30,000, less any expenses allowance the court considers just, and owes nothing more. Each side otherwise bears its own losses.

questions.q: Polaris Shipping Ltd agreed to carry 50,000 tonnes of grain for Danube Grain plc from Odesa to Alexandria within a 'shipment window' in March, at a freight of $2 million. Polaris owns two suitable vessels, the Vega and the Rigel. It had also agreed to carry cargo for another customer, Orion, in March. In February, the Vega was seized by authorities in a dispute unrelated to either contract. Polaris used the Rigel for Orion's cargo and told Danube the contract was frustrated. Danube had chartered a warehouse in Alexandria for £150,000, which it has now lost. The contract contained a clause excusing Polaris for 'arrest or restraint of princes', requiring Polaris to use reasonable endeavours to avoid or overcome the event. Advise Danube.
markScheme: Identifies that the contract provides for the event: force majeure clause is the starting point; frustration cannot apply where the contract makes provision for the event.
Construction of the clause: 'arrest or restraint of princes' likely covers seizure; burden on Polaris to show the event caused the non-performance.

Reasonable endeavours: whether Polaris had to use the Rigel or obtain a substitute; MUR Shipping v RTI (2024) – reasonable endeavours do not require departing from the contract's terms, but here using available vessels is within performance.
Causation: the seizure did not itself prevent performance where an alternative vessel was available; Polaris's choice caused the failure.
Self-induced frustration: The Super Servant Two (1990) – electing between contracts after losing a vessel is not frustration; Maritime National Fish (1935).
Concludes Polaris cannot rely on frustration and probably not the clause; its refusal is a breach and, by declaring the contract frustrated, a repudiation.
Danube's remedies: damages for breach; expectation measure; remoteness of the warehouse cost (Hadley v Baxendale (1854) limb 1/2) and mitigation.
Notes the 1943 Act does not apply to carriage of goods by sea contracts (s2(5)(a)), so it would not govern even if frustrated.
Considers alternative argument Polaris may raise: that the clause applies and the reasonable endeavours duty did not require it to break the Orion contract; evaluates.
Clear conclusion and structure.
questions.modelAnswer:
Starting point: the contract's own terms. Where the contract deals with an event, frustration generally cannot apply, so Polaris's first argument must be the force majeure clause. Seizure of a vessel by authorities probably falls within 'arrest or restraint of princes'. But Polaris must also show that the event caused its failure to perform, and that it used reasonable endeavours to avoid or overcome it.

Causation and reasonable endeavours. The contract was to carry grain within a window, apparently without naming the Vega. Polaris had a second suitable vessel, the Rigel. The seizure therefore did not prevent performance. What prevented it was Polaris's decision to use the Rigel for Orion. MUR Shipping v RTI (2024) held that reasonable endeavours did not require the affected party to accept performance on terms different from the contract, there by taking payment in another currency. Here, by contrast, using the Rigel to perform this contract would mean performing the contract on its own terms, so it is the kind of step reasonable endeavours would ordinarily require. Polaris will argue it could not perform both contracts and should not have to break Orion's contract. But it took on both commitments knowing it had two vessels. The clause is therefore unlikely to excuse it.

Frustration. Even if the clause did not apply, frustration fails. In The Super Servant Two (1990), a carrier that lost one of two vessels and chose to use the other for different contracts could not claim frustration: the failure resulted from its own election. The non-performance is self-induced.

Consequences. Polaris has failed to perform and, by declaring the contract frustrated, has shown it will not perform, which is a repudiation. Danube can accept it and claim damages. The expectation measure covers the extra cost of alternative shipping and losses caused by delay. The £150,000 warehouse cost is recoverable if it was within reasonable contemplation. Storage at the destination is a natural consequence of a carriage contract (Hadley v Baxendale (1854); Victoria Laundry (1949)). Danube must mitigate, for example by sub-letting the warehouse if possible.

Finally, even if the contract were frustrated, the 1943 Act would not apply, because s2(5)(a) excludes most contracts for carriage of goods by sea, so the common law would govern the money.

Conclusion: Polaris cannot rely on frustration or, probably, the clause. Danube should treat the contract as repudiated and claim damages.

questions.q: 'The doctrine of frustration is so narrow that it is practically irrelevant to commercial parties, who must rely on force majeure clauses instead. Where it does apply, the Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 produces arbitrary results.' Critically discuss both parts of this statement.
markScheme: Explains the theoretical basis: implied term (Taylor v Caldwell (1863)) versus construction/radical difference (Davis Contractors (1956)); The Sea Angel (2007) multi-factorial approach.
Demonstrates narrowness: Tsakiroglou (1962); Davis Contractors; Amalgamated Investment v John Walker (1977); Canary Wharf v EMA (2019); self-induced frustration (Super Servant Two (1990)).

Acknowledges when frustration still applies: destruction of subject matter, supervening illegality (Fibrosa (1943)), cancellation of the purpose (Krell v Henry (1903)), and its residual role as a backstop where clauses do not cover the event.

Discusses force majeure clauses: depend on drafting; burden on the party relying on them; causation and mitigation requirements; MUR Shipping (2024); clauses often more flexible (suspension, notice, renegotiation).
Evaluates whether narrowness is justified: sanctity of contract, parties' ability to allocate risk, commercial certainty.
LR(FC)A s1(2): broad discretion on expenses, capped at sums paid/payable; Gamerco (1995) shows unpredictability.
s1(3): BP v Hunt (1979) valuation by end product; harsh results if the product is destroyed; criticism of how the Act allocates loss.
Exclusions (s2(5)) and contracting out (s2(3)) limit the Act's reach.
Considers reform proposals or alternative models (loss-sharing; comparative approaches such as hardship doctrines).
Reasoned conclusion engaging both parts.
questions.modelAnswer:
The first claim is that frustration is too narrow to matter. The implied-condition theory of Taylor v Caldwell (1863) has given way to the radical difference test of Davis Contractors (1956). The Sea Angel (2007) added a multi-factorial analysis. The doctrine is undeniably narrow. Delay and expense do not suffice (Davis; Tsakiroglou (1962)). Events within the risk taken on by a party do not count (Amalgamated Investment v John Walker (1977)). Even Brexit did not frustrate the European Medicines Agency's lease (Canary Wharf v EMA (2019)). Self-induced events are excluded (The Super Servant Two (1990)).

Yet 'practically irrelevant' goes too far. Frustration still operates in clear cases: destruction of the subject matter, supervening illegality such as wartime trading bans (Fibrosa (1943)), and the failure of a shared purpose (Krell v Henry (1903)). It remains a necessary backstop for events no clause covers. Force majeure clauses are central in practice but depend on drafting, and the party relying on one must prove the event falls within it and caused the failure; MUR Shipping (2024) shows the wording controls. Their advantage is flexibility: they can suspend obligations or trigger renegotiation.

The second claim concerns the 1943 Act. Under s1(2), money paid is recoverable, and the court may let the payee keep a sum for expenses, capped at what was paid or payable before discharge. The broad discretion makes outcomes hard to predict: Gamerco (1995) ordered full repayment with no deduction. A payee to whom nothing was paid or payable before discharge gets nothing for expenses. Under s1(3), BP v Hunt (1979) values the benefit by its end product as affected by the frustrating event. A builder whose partly built structure is destroyed may recover nothing despite extensive work. The Act also excludes major commercial categories (s2(5)) and allows contracting out (s2(3)).

Results thus depend on the timing of payments and survival of the end product rather than any principled view of loss-sharing. Reform options include a general power to apportion losses, or a civil-law-style hardship doctrine, though both reduce predictability.

In conclusion, frustration is narrow by design and force majeure clauses do most of the work, but the doctrine remains a valuable residual safety net. The 1943 Act is fairly criticised for haphazard results. The best reform would be clearer guidance on loss allocation rather than a wider doctrine of frustration.

questions.q: Breach of which type of term always entitles the innocent party to terminate the contract, regardless of the consequences of the breach?
options: A warranty
An innominate term
A condition
An implied term in fact
questions.why: Breach of a condition entitles the innocent party to terminate whatever the consequences. For an innominate term, it depends on the seriousness of the breach (Hongkong Fir (1962)); for a warranty, damages only.

questions.q: A seller declares that it will not deliver goods due in June. The buyer, in May, tells the seller it will keep the contract alive and await delivery. Before June, the buyer itself commits a repudiatory breach. Which statement is correct?
options: The seller remains liable because it repudiated first
The buyer's affirmation kept the contract alive for both parties, so the seller can rely on the buyer's later breach
The buyer can still claim damages for the original repudiation at any time
The contract was automatically terminated by the seller's repudiation
questions.why: Under Fercometal v MSC (The Simona) (1989), affirmation keeps the contract alive for the benefit of both parties. The repudiating party can then take advantage of later events, including the innocent party's own breach.

questions.q: What is anticipatory breach, and what options does the innocent party have?
markScheme: Anticipatory breach occurs when a party, before performance is due, clearly indicates it will not perform, or disables itself from performing (Hochster v De la Tour (1853)).
The innocent party may accept the repudiation, terminate and sue immediately, or affirm the contract and await performance (but then remains bound).
questions.modelAnswer: Anticipatory breach occurs when, before performance is due, one party makes clear by words or conduct that it will not perform, or puts it out of its power to perform. In Hochster v De la Tour (1853), a courier was told before his start date that he would not be needed, and he could sue at once. The innocent party has a choice. It can accept the repudiation, end the contract and claim damages immediately. Or it can affirm and wait for the performance date, but then the contract stays alive for both sides.

questions.q: Explain the rule in White & Carter (Councils) v McGregor (1962) and its limits.
markScheme: Facts: advertising contract repudiated on the day it was made; the claimants went ahead, displayed the adverts and claimed the price.
Rule: an innocent party may refuse to accept a repudiation, perform and claim the agreed sum.
Limits: performance must be possible without the other party's cooperation.

Limits: the innocent party must have a legitimate interest in performing rather than claiming damages; no legitimate interest where performance is wholly unreasonable (The Alaskan Trader (1984); MSC Mediterranean Shipping v Cottonex (2016)).
questions.modelAnswer: In White & Carter v McGregor (1962), a garage owner cancelled a three-year advertising contract on the day it was signed. The agency ignored this, displayed the adverts and recovered the full price. An innocent party need not accept a repudiation: it may perform and claim the agreed sum. Lord Reid set two limits. Performance must be possible without the other party's cooperation, and the innocent party must have a legitimate interest in performing rather than claiming damages. In The Alaskan Trader (1984), owners keeping a ship ready for a charterer with no use for it lacked such an interest. MSC v Cottonex (2016) confirms the right is lost where insisting on performance is wholly unreasonable.

questions.q: Sterling Foods Ltd contracted to buy 1,000 cases of tinned tomatoes per month for 12 months from Valley Produce Ltd, 'to be shipped in good condition'. Clause 6 provided: 'Delivery by the 5th of each month is a condition of this contract.' In month 3, the delivery arrived on the 6th. In month 4, 30 of the 1,000 cases were dented but the tins inside were usable; Sterling sold them at a discount and lost £400. Tomato prices have since fallen sharply, and Sterling wants to terminate the contract and buy elsewhere. Advise Sterling.
markScheme: Classifies terms: conditions, warranties and innominate terms; consequences of each.
Clause 6: express designation as a 'condition'; time clauses in mercantile contracts are generally conditions (Bunge v Tradax (1981)).
Considers Schuler v Wickman (1974): the label is not conclusive if the result would be unreasonable, but in a commercial sale with a clear designation, courts usually respect it.
One-day late delivery therefore likely a breach of condition entitling termination – subject to whether Sterling affirmed by accepting month 3's delivery and continuing.

Instalment contracts: whether breach of one instalment entitles termination of the whole (SGA 1979 s31(2): depends on terms and circumstances, ratio of breach to whole and likelihood of repetition – Maple Flock v Universal Furniture (1934)).

'Shipped in good condition' as an innominate term (Cehave v Bremer (The Hansa Nord) (1976)); minor damage to 3% of one delivery does not deprive Sterling of substantially the whole benefit; damages of £400.
SGA s15A: in non-consumer sales, slight breach of implied quality terms cannot justify rejection.
Notes that the motive of escaping a falling market is irrelevant if a right to terminate exists (Arcos v Ronaasen (1933)), though courts dislike it.
Reasoned conclusion with practical advice (risk of wrongful termination being itself a repudiation).
questions.modelAnswer:
Classification. Breach of a condition allows termination whatever the consequences. Breach of a warranty gives only damages. For an innominate term, termination is available only if the breach deprives the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit of the contract (Hongkong Fir (1962)).

Late delivery in month 3. Clause 6 expressly calls timely delivery a condition. In commercial contracts, time clauses are generally treated as conditions because certainty matters (Bunge v Tradax (1981)). Schuler v Wickman (1974) shows the label is not conclusive where treating every trivial breach as a condition would be unreasonable. But in a commercial sale where the parties clearly intended timing to be essential, a court will usually respect the designation. Two problems remain for Sterling. First, it accepted the month-3 delivery and continued with the contract, which may amount to affirmation, losing the right to terminate for that breach. Second, this is an instalment contract. Under s31(2) of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, whether a breach in one instalment justifies ending the whole contract depends on the terms and circumstances. Maple Flock v Universal Furniture (1934) emphasised how much of the contract the breach affects and how likely it is to recur. However, an express condition covering each monthly delivery is a strong signal that any late delivery allows termination. Sterling's best argument is that clause 6 entitles it to terminate. Its weakness is that it did not act promptly after month 3.

Damaged cases in month 4. 'Shipped in good condition' is likely an innominate term, as in Cehave v Bremer (The Hansa Nord) (1976). Dents to 3% of one delivery, with usable contents, do not deprive Sterling of substantially the whole benefit. Any claim under the implied quality term in s14 would also be limited by s15A, which prevents rejection for slight breaches in non-consumer sales. Sterling's remedy is damages of £400.

Motive. Sterling's real reason is the falling market. If a legal right to terminate exists, motive does not matter (Arcos v Ronaasen (1933)). But if Sterling terminates without such a right, it will itself repudiate the contract and be liable to Valley.

Advice. Sterling should claim £400 for the damaged cases. Its right to terminate depends on clause 6 and whether it affirmed after month 3. The safest course is to reserve its rights expressly and terminate only if a further late delivery occurs.

questions.q: Kestrel Builders contracted with Aisha to build a garden studio for £60,000, payable on completion. Kestrel finished the studio, but the floor was slightly uneven, which would cost £1,500 to fix, and the windows were of a cheaper brand than specified, though of similar quality. Aisha refused to pay anything. Separately, Kestrel had agreed to build a garage for Ben for £30,000, also payable on completion. Halfway through, Ben told Kestrel he had changed his mind and did not want the garage. Kestrel ignored this, finished the garage over Ben's objections (it had access to Ben's land under the contract), and now claims £30,000. Advise Kestrel.
markScheme: Aisha: entire obligation – payment on completion (Cutter v Powell (1795)); strict rule that partial or defective performance earns nothing.
Doctrine of substantial performance: Hoenig v Isaacs (1952) – price payable less cost of remedying defects; contrast Bolton v Mahadeva (1972).

Applies: £1,500 defect on £60,000 job plus window substitution of similar quality – substantial performance likely; Kestrel recovers £60,000 less £1,500 and any loss from the windows (possibly nominal, or Ruxley-type amenity loss).
Notes Aisha cannot keep the studio without paying; alternatively considers whether she accepted the work.
Ben: repudiation before completion; Kestrel's election to affirm and perform (White & Carter v McGregor (1962)).
Cooperation requirement: Kestrel did not need Ben's cooperation because it had contractual access to the land.
Legitimate interest limit: The Alaskan Trader (1984); MSC v Cottonex (2016); whether completing an unwanted garage was wholly unreasonable compared with damages.
If Kestrel had no legitimate interest, it is limited to damages: loss of profit plus costs incurred to the date of repudiation, minus savings.
Discusses mitigation does not apply to an action for an agreed sum, unless the White & Carter limits are engaged.
Reasoned conclusion on both claims.
questions.modelAnswer:
Aisha. Payment on completion suggests an entire obligation. On the strict view in Cutter v Powell (1795), Kestrel would recover nothing unless it performed exactly. However, Hoenig v Isaacs (1952) holds that where a lump-sum contract for work and materials has been substantially performed, the contractor can recover the price less the cost of fixing defects. In Hoenig, defects costing about £56 on a £750 job did not defeat the claim. By contrast, in Bolton v Mahadeva (1972), central heating that gave off fumes and heated poorly, costing nearly a third of the price to fix, was not substantial performance. Here the studio is complete. The £1,500 floor defect is 2.5% of the price, and the windows are of similar quality though not the specified brand. That is substantial performance. Kestrel can recover £60,000 less £1,500 for the floor. For the windows, Aisha can claim damages for the departure from the specification. If replacing them would be disproportionate and they are of equal value, damages may be small, possibly a modest sum for loss of amenity by analogy with Ruxley v Forsyth (1996).

Ben. Ben repudiated the contract when he said he no longer wanted the garage. Kestrel could accept the repudiation and claim damages, or affirm and continue. Under White & Carter v McGregor (1962), it may perform and claim the agreed price, subject to two limits. First, performance must be possible without Ben's cooperation. The contract gave Kestrel access to Ben's land, so that is satisfied. Second, Kestrel must have a legitimate interest in performing rather than claiming damages. The Alaskan Trader (1984) and MSC v Cottonex (2016) show that there is no legitimate interest where insisting on performance is wholly unreasonable and damages are adequate. Completing an unwanted garage simply to run up the price looks close to that line. Kestrel's damages would be readily calculable: lost profit plus costs incurred, minus savings. Kestrel may cite its interest in keeping its workforce employed, but courts are reluctant to allow wasteful performance where damages suffice.

If the White & Carter right applies, Kestrel recovers £30,000 as a debt, free of mitigation rules; if not, it gets only damages assessed at the repudiation.

Conclusion: Kestrel will recover most of the studio price from Aisha. Its claim for Ben's full price is uncertain and may be reduced to damages.

questions.q: What is the basic aim of an award of damages for breach of contract?
options: To punish the party in breach
To restore the claimant to the position it was in before the contract
To put the claimant in the position it would have been in had the contract been performed
To strip the defendant of any profit made from the breach
questions.why: Robinson v Harman (1848): contract damages protect the expectation interest. Reliance damages (pre-contract position) are an alternative measure, and gain-based awards are exceptional.

questions.q: Under the test in Cavendish Square Holding v Makdessi and ParkingEye v Beavis (2015), when is a clause requiring payment of a sum on breach unenforceable as a penalty?
options: Whenever the sum exceeds a genuine pre-estimate of the innocent party's loss
When it imposes a detriment out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in performance
Whenever one party had stronger bargaining power
Whenever the clause appears in standard terms
questions.why: The Supreme Court restated the test as whether the detriment is out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance. A genuine pre-estimate of loss is sufficient but not necessary.

questions.q: A defendant breaches a restrictive covenant not to compete. The claimant's financial loss from lost profits can be calculated with reasonable precision. Following Morris-Garner v One Step (Support) (2018), which remedy is the claimant most likely to receive?
options: Negotiating damages, assessed as a hypothetical release fee
An account of the defendant's profits as of right
Compensatory damages for lost profits
Nominal damages only
questions.why: Morris-Garner held that negotiating damages are not available where ordinary financial loss can be quantified. They are reserved for cases where the breached right was a valuable asset whose loss is measured that way. An account of profits is exceptional (AG v Blake (2001)).

questions.q: Explain the remoteness test in contract, distinguishing the two limbs of Hadley v Baxendale (1854).
markScheme: Limb 1: loss arising naturally, in the usual course of things, from the breach is recoverable.

Limb 2: loss arising from special circumstances is recoverable only if those circumstances were known to or communicated to both parties so that the loss was within their reasonable contemplation at the time of contracting (Victoria Laundry (1949)).
