The degree of probability: loss must be 'not unlikely' or a serious possibility (The Heron II (1969)), a stricter test than tort's reasonable foreseeability.
questions.modelAnswer: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) limits recovery to losses within two categories. Under limb 1, losses that arise naturally, in the usual course of things, from the breach are recoverable, because every contracting party is presumed to know them. Under limb 2, losses arising from special circumstances are recoverable only if the defendant knew of those circumstances when the contract was made, so that the loss was within both parties' reasonable contemplation. In Victoria Laundry (1949), ordinary laundry profits were recoverable but unusually lucrative dyeing contracts unknown to the defendant were not. The Heron II (1969) requires the loss to have been 'not unlikely' or a serious possibility, which is stricter than the reasonable foreseeability test in tort.

questions.q: When will a court order specific performance of a contract, and when will it refuse?
markScheme: Specific performance is an equitable, discretionary remedy granted where damages are inadequate.
Examples where damages inadequate: land, unique goods, and where damages would be only nominal (Beswick v Beswick (1968)).
Bars: contracts for personal services, and contracts needing constant supervision (Co-operative Insurance v Argyll Stores (1998)).
Other equitable bars: delay, unclean hands, hardship, and lack of mutuality; specific performance of a sale of goods also available under SGA 1979 s52.
questions.modelAnswer: Specific performance is an equitable, discretionary order to perform, granted where damages are inadequate. That is presumed for land, applies to unique goods (see also Sale of Goods Act 1979 s52), and in Beswick v Beswick (1968) it was ordered because damages to the estate would have been nominal. Courts refuse it for personal service contracts, and where the order would need constant supervision: in Co-operative Insurance v Argyll Stores (1998), the House of Lords would not order a supermarket to keep trading. Delay, unclean hands and severe hardship can also lead to refusal.

questions.q: 'The penalty rule is an indefensible restriction on freedom of contract.' Evaluate this claim in light of Cavendish Square Holding v Makdessi (2015).
markScheme: Explains the rule: courts will not enforce a secondary obligation triggered by breach that is out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest.

Cavendish replaced the 'genuine pre-estimate of loss' focus of Dunlop v New Garage (1915) with a broader legitimate interest test, recognising interests beyond compensation (e.g. ParkingEye's interest in managing parking).
The Supreme Court considered and rejected abolishing the rule, and also rejected extending it to primary obligations (contrast the Australian approach in Andrews v ANZ (2012)).
Arguments for the claim: commercial parties can price and allocate risk; the rule creates uncertainty; it is easily avoided by drafting obligations as primary rather than secondary.

Arguments against: protects weaker parties against oppressive terms; consumer protection overlap with CRA 2015; Cavendish's deference to negotiated terms between sophisticated parties limits interference.
Conclusion: the rule is a narrow, defensible control, though the primary/secondary distinction is formalistic.
questions.modelAnswer: The rule stops enforcement of a clause triggered by breach where the detriment is out of all proportion to the innocent party's legitimate interest in performance. Cavendish (2015) kept the rule but replaced the 'genuine pre-estimate' focus of Dunlop (1915) with a wider legitimate interest test, so ParkingEye's £85 charge was upheld. The court refused to extend the rule to primary obligations, unlike Andrews v ANZ (2012) in Australia. Critics say sophisticated parties should price risk freely, and that the rule is uncertain and easily drafted around. But it guards against oppressive terms, and courts now presume negotiated clauses valid. It is a narrow, defensible control; its weak point is the formal primary/secondary distinction.

questions.q: Rafael, a wedding photographer, contracted with Hart Cameras Ltd to buy a specialist camera for £4,000, with delivery on 1 June. He told Hart's salesperson that he needed it for a high-profile celebrity wedding on 5 June, for which he would be paid £12,000. Hart delivered on 8 June. Rafael had to cancel the wedding booking, losing the £12,000 fee. He also missed out on a magazine deal worth £30,000, which he had been negotiating privately and had not mentioned to Hart. He spent £600 on travel to Hart's warehouse trying to collect the camera. Rafael was very upset by the whole episode. A comparable camera could have been hired for £500 for the wedding. Advise Rafael on the damages he can recover.
markScheme: States the expectation principle (Robinson v Harman (1848)).
Remoteness: Hadley v Baxendale (1854) limbs; the £12,000 wedding fee was communicated, so within limb 2 (reasonable contemplation).
The £30,000 magazine deal was not communicated; like the dyeing contracts in Victoria Laundry (1949), not recoverable as a special loss.
Considers whether some loss of ordinary further work is limb 1; type versus extent of loss (Parsons v Uttley Ingham (1978)).

Mitigation (British Westinghouse (1912); Payzu v Saunders (1919)): Rafael could have hired a comparable camera for £500; his recovery may be limited to that hire cost rather than the £12,000 lost fee.
The £600 travel costs: recoverable if a reasonable attempt to mitigate or consequence of breach.

Mental distress: generally not recoverable (Addis (1909)); exceptions for contracts whose object is pleasure or peace of mind (Jarvis (1973); Farley v Skinner (2001)) not applicable to a commercial camera purchase.
Reasoned conclusion with likely figures.
questions.modelAnswer:
The aim is to put Rafael in the position he would have been in had the camera arrived on time (Robinson v Harman (1848)), subject to remoteness and mitigation.

The £12,000 wedding fee. Lost earnings from a particular booking would not ordinarily be within limb 1 of Hadley v Baxendale (1854). But Rafael told Hart's salesperson about the wedding and the fee before contracting. That makes the loss within the parties' reasonable contemplation under limb 2, and a serious possibility if delivery were late (The Heron II (1969)). It is not too remote.

The £30,000 magazine deal. Rafael kept this to himself. As in Victoria Laundry (1949), where the defendant did not know about especially lucrative government contracts, the loss arose from special circumstances unknown to Hart. Rafael might argue that some further work was a natural consequence, and Parsons v Uttley Ingham (1978) holds that if the type of loss is contemplated, its extent need not be. But an unknown, unusually valuable deal is unlikely to be treated as the same type of loss as an ordinary booking. It is irrecoverable.

Mitigation. Rafael cannot recover loss he could reasonably have avoided (British Westinghouse (1912)). A comparable camera could have been hired for £500. If that option was reasonably available to him, the court will treat the £12,000 loss as avoidable, and he will recover only the £500 hire cost. Payzu v Saunders (1919) shows the court expects sensible commercial steps. If Rafael can show he did not know of the hire option, or that hiring was not practical in time, he may recover the full £12,000. The burden is on Hart to show he failed to mitigate.

The £600 travel. Travel costs incurred trying to collect the camera are a reasonable response to the breach and a natural consequence, so they are recoverable.

Distress. Damages for disappointment are generally unavailable (Addis v Gramophone (1909)). The exceptions in Jarvis v Swans Tours (1973) and Farley v Skinner (2001) apply where a major object of the contract is pleasure or peace of mind. Buying a work camera is a commercial transaction, so no award is likely.

Conclusion: Rafael is likely to recover £600 plus either £500 (if hire was reasonably available) or £12,000 (if not), but nothing for the magazine deal or distress.

questions.q: Grange Developments Ltd bought a plot of land from Thornfield Estates in 2019, covenanting not to build more than 20 houses on it. In breach, Grange built 30 houses, making an extra profit of £1.2 million. Thornfield's adjoining land has not fallen in value, and Thornfield cannot show any financial loss. The houses are now occupied by purchasers. Thornfield seeks (a) an injunction ordering demolition of the extra 10 houses, (b) an account of Grange's £1.2 million profit, or (c) some other monetary remedy. Advise Thornfield, critically evaluating whether English law adequately protects a contracting party's performance interest where breach causes no measurable financial loss.
markScheme: Identifies the performance interest problem: expectation damages based on financial loss would give nominal damages.

Injunction: mandatory injunction to demolish – courts will consider whether damages in lieu are appropriate; occupation by third-party purchasers and waste (Wrotham Park Estate v Parkside Homes (1974) refused demolition); Senior Courts Act 1981 s50 power to award damages in lieu.

Account of profits: AG v Blake (2001) – exceptional remedy where other remedies are inadequate and the claimant has a legitimate interest in preventing profit; commercial breaches rarely qualify (Experience Hendrix v PPX (2003) awarded a licence fee rather than full account).

Negotiating damages: Wrotham Park (5% of profit); Morris-Garner v One Step (2018) – available where the breach results in loss of a valuable asset created or protected by the right, classic example being restrictive covenants over land.
Applies: Thornfield likely to obtain negotiating damages based on a hypothetical release fee reasonably negotiated before breach, considering Grange's anticipated profit.
Discusses how the hypothetical bargain is valued (Lunn Poly; Pell Frischmann v Bow Valley (2009); One Step); likely a proportion of £1.2m.
Considers cost-of-cure and loss of amenity analogies (Ruxley (1996)).

Evaluation: the performance interest (Lord Goff and Lord Millett in Alfred McAlpine v Panatown (2001); academic writing, e.g. Friedmann/Coote), efficient breach theory, and whether gain-based awards undermine the compensatory principle.
Assesses Morris-Garner's characterisation of negotiating damages as compensatory versus restitutionary; criticisms of artificiality.
Reasoned conclusion on remedies and the evaluative question.
questions.modelAnswer:
Thornfield has suffered no measurable financial loss. A narrow compensatory approach would give only nominal damages while Grange keeps £1.2 million made by breaking its promise. The case tests how far English law protects the 'performance interest', the interest in receiving what was bargained for.

(a) Injunction. A mandatory demolition order is discretionary, and s50 of the Senior Courts Act 1981 lets the court award damages instead. In Wrotham Park Estate v Parkside Homes (1974), Brightman J refused to order demolition of houses built in breach of covenant because it would waste much-needed housing. With innocent purchasers in occupation, demolition is very unlikely.

(b) Account of profits. AG v Blake (2001) allows an account only in exceptional cases, where other remedies are inadequate and the claimant has a legitimate interest in preventing the defendant's profit. Blake concerned a former spy in a relationship close to a fiduciary one. In commercial cases, courts have preferred a reasonable fee (Experience Hendrix v PPX (2003)). A full account of £1.2 million is unlikely.

(c) Negotiating damages. This is Thornfield's best claim. Wrotham Park awarded 5% of the developer's anticipated profit as a hypothetical release fee. Morris-Garner v One Step (2018) confirmed that such damages are available where the breach causes the loss of a valuable asset created or protected by the right, and a restrictive covenant over land is the paradigm example. The court values a release negotiated reasonably just before the breach, taking account of Grange's anticipated profit. Thornfield should recover a substantial share of the profit, though not all of it.

Evaluation. Efficient breach theorists argue that Grange should be free to break the covenant if it pays for any loss, so nominal damages are correct. But that treats a promise as a mere option to pay, lets the party in breach keep the whole gain, and undermines the security of bargains. Morris-Garner protects the performance interest by treating the covenant itself as an asset whose loss is compensable, while insisting the award is compensatory, not restitutionary. Critics call the release fee a fiction and say a candid gain-based measure would be more honest.

Conclusion: Thornfield should not expect demolition or a full account, but should recover substantial negotiating damages. The law protects the performance interest well for property-type rights such as land covenants, but less clearly for ordinary promises where loss is hard to prove.
